There were some points of difference, and maybe that was more cultural than anything, but when you look at the numbers it turns out that the outcomes were identical.
The health outcomes?
Lord Offord of Garvel : The health outcomes.
Q75 What about economic outcomes? Was there any effect i n respect of the differences and how much the different areas were affected?

Lord Offord of Garvel : Again, we look at the economic data between the UK and Scotland and we find it is pretty much identical. If anything, Scotland is a little bit ahead in GDP recovery. It is quite interesting that we had different messaging — for example , the UK was hands, face, space and Scotland had FACT S . Do you remember what they were?
Face, wear —I just us ed hands, face, space, quite frankly. It did the same job.
Lord Offord of Garvel : Maybe the Chair can remember.
FACTS was hard to remember.
Lord Offord of Garvel : What was FACTS in Scotland?
I think let him get on and ask his questions of you, Minister. It was a good attempt, anyway. Have you finished, David?
That was the end of my questions, since I could not answer the Minister’s question.

Q76 Can I start by correcting the Chair? The Chair said this was our final evidence session in this inquiry, but of course we hope it is not, because we have now had three refusals from the Deputy First Minister of Scotland, Shona Rob i son , to appear before this inquiry. I am very grateful that we have a UK Government Minister here. We all as a Committee have tried to get a member of the Scottish Government in front of us— indeed , the Chair , as an SNP Member, has told us that he has personally tried. It is going to be very difficult for us to do a report on this issue if we only hear from one side, so hopefully your presence here today, Minister, will finally encourage a Scottish Government representative to attend.

That is where I want to start, perhaps following on from David Duguid’s points. There were undoubtedly differences in the way the funding was spent, and you have made it very clear that funding was given by the UK Government to the Scottish Government and they could take their own decisions. You have also done a lot of outreach in Scotland in your ministerial roles. Did you pick up any concerns from businesses about that differentiation? Certainly, what we heard last week from the Federation of Small Business es was that in many cases they would have liked a UK-wide approach, so businesses in England would have received the same support as businesses in Scotland. Is that something that you have picked up?

Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes, there were grumbles. That is the issue when you have slight differences between regions : some are better and some are worse. I personally would have favoured a completely uniform approach. In the main it was mostly uniform but, yes, there were grumbles from the small business community and the self-employed and from the farming community. That again I think is a very valid level of inquiry for the Scottish covid inquiry, because I think that is where the Scottish covid inquiry needs to drill in, to see if where Scotland did diverge from the UK it was better or worse.

Q77 Are you aware of any reasons why the Scottish Government diverge d from the UK Government’s decisions, other than to be slightly different? Were the Scotland Office informed of legitimate and good reasons to take a different path ? O r were you and everyone else aware that certain businesses would not be covered by something that was covered elsewhere in the UK?

Lord Offord of Garvel : We did not come across any particular reason. Our emphasis at the Scotland Office , given that Scotland, with 8% of the population and 33% of the geography , has a greater number of remote communities , was that we were very focused on making sure that we had uniform treatment wherever people lived in Scotland. We were very focused on that. We did not see any particular evidence as to why a small business in Motherwell was different to a small business in Warrington. We did not see any circumstantial evidence on that.

Q78 Another thing that we are looking at , and the Auditor General in Scotland has also looked at, is the full amount of covid support passed from the UK Government to the Scottish Government being spent for covid support in Scotland. Are you concerned that the Auditor General in Scotland has been unable to qualify the entire amount of money that has gone from the UK Government to the Scottish Government and to see whether it was fully s p ent on covid -related issues? I think the figure is £1.6 billion that he has been unable to attribute to that.

Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes, of course. That is why I say it is the most extraordinary concept of devolution that you would not get in the German federal system or the US federal system. When Washington sends money to individual states, they want an audit of it — they want to know where it was spent. It is extraordinary in the UK that it is a completely devolved scenario and the Barnett consequentials and the block grant goes from London to Edinburgh with no strings attached.

Q79 What is the UK Government’s response to that Auditor General report? Do you then follow that up? Do you look at this further? I understand that decisions had to be taken very quickly and t hat t o get money out to support as many people as possible it wa s the right approach for the UK Government to take , but there are businesses and individuals in Scotland who still feel they should have received that funding and are very upset to find that the Scottish Auditor General is unable to account for all that money.
Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes, and this is a question that is now being asked repeatedly in the Chamber in which I reside.

Q80 I think it is slightly different — I do not want to go there because I think that is more generally on spending . On covid spending in particular, if I could ask about an example, I think we have both met Scotland’s Learning Partnership , and t hey have serious concerns that they were promised by John Swinney, Richard Loch h ead and other Ministers that they were going to get money that had been given by the UK Government to the Scottish Government, and they did not and still have not received that funding. Is that your recollection of your meetings with them?

Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes and , in fact , coming back to Wendy Chamberlain’s question about the economically inactive, they are front and centre in this battle to help our most vulnerable back into work, who want to work. It is all to do with adult learning ; it is all to do with retraining. That is where we need to put a lot of focus, and we both agree that the best form of welfare one can ever have is a good job. There are people in that adult community who want to get a good job and need help to get there, and that particular community — that particular group — I was so impressed when I met them, that that is what their life’s work is, yet they are starved of funding.
But funding that they believe they were entitled to .
Lord Offord of Garvel : That they were promised.

Q81 I ndeed , I think they have shown me some correspondence — which I am quite happy to share with the Committee —in which they have been given assurances from several Scottish Government Ministers that they would receive that covid funding, and they still have not. That then does beg the question of whether that is part of the £1.6 billion that the Auditor General cannot account for.
Lord Offord of Garvel : This is where I would expect the Scotland covid inquiry to make a full inquiry.
Q82 It would also be an opportunity for the Deputy First Minister of Scotland to answer these questions, if she attended this Committee.
Lord Offord of Garvel : I will recommend this Committee to her when I see her later .
Q83 Hopefully that will work where other efforts have not.

The Chair mentioned Brexit and was surprised that it had not been raised in the opening seven minutes of this inquiry session. Maybe that is because th e inquiry is not about Brexit; it is about coronavirus. I want to look at coronavirus and Europe. Y ou mentioned the vaccine roll-out; is it the UK Government’s view that we would have had as fast and as successful a vaccine roll-out in Scotland and across the UK if we were still part of the EU?

Lord Offord of Garvel : That is not a matter of opinion : i t is self-evident that because we had come out of the EU we were able to then plot our own response, which we would not have been able to do. We would have had to go with the EU-wide scheme. If you remember , at one point the French and the Germans were very annoyed with the UK because we had stolen a march on them, and we had put our money down and signed contracts and procured ourselves early supplies of the vaccines, which we would not have been able to do if we had been part of the EU. It is not a matter of opinion; it is a matter of fact that we were able to proceed faster.
Q84 That then also allowed us to lift the restrictions across the UK and slightly later i n Scotland because more people were protected quicker than other parts of the EU and around the world.
Lord Offord of Garvel : Correct.

Q85 Which , therefore , allowed our economy to hopefully get in a better position at an earlier stage, because people were getting out and about more, being able to spend money, and get back to work .

Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes. But if you take the fact that the three high - spending economies were the US, the UK and New Zealand, they are independent countries so they were perhaps able to do their individual responses but act fast, spend the most amount of money and came out perhaps the quickest.

Q86 Finally, how do you view the relations between the Scottish and the UK Government s during the pandemic? As you said earlier, t here was a time in the pandemic whe n they worked very closely, and it then started to diverge a bit more as the pandemic continued. Were there opportunities that were missed for better collaboration between the two Governments ? I s that a lesson that this Committee can look at in our inquiry report? Could there have been better working relations between the two Governments to provide a more unified response to the pandemic?

Lord Offord of Garvel : As I said , the response financially and from a health point of view was UK-wide, even to the point of the UK armed services being deployed in Scotland as much as, if not more so, than in England. There were inter-governmental l meetings going on and former colleague and former Minister David Duguid would have been involved in that. I personally was not involved at that moment, but the record shows there was a lot of inter-governmental interaction on these decisions.

Ultimately, again through the devolution settlement, the Scottish Government wanted to set their own tone, their own messaging —we are back to FACTS — and wanted to finesse some schemes. All I am observing at the end of it is they were perhaps on the margin. The overall response was uniform, and the outcome was uniform. Scotland’s outcomes ended up being the same as the UK’s .

Q87 Good afternoon, Lord Offord. It is interesting to hear Mr Ross raise the issue of covid because I know that in an evidence session recently of the UK covid inquiry, they were told that planning for a no-deal Brexit crowded out efforts of the UK Government to prepare for a pandemic, which was something — [ Interruption. ] I do not know why I am being interrupted. I stayed quiet during—
Lord Offord of Garvel : Sorry, can you repeat that?
Order. Let us a sk questions and answer questions, please .
Can we start the clock again, perhaps, Mr Wishart? Thank you.

The recent first evidence session of the UK covid inquiry heard that planning for a no-deal Brexit crowded out efforts that the UK Government were making to prepare for a pandemic . P reparations for Operation Yellowhammer I think were specifically referenced. That was a point that was echoed by the former First Minister of Scotland when she gave evidence at the same inquiry. As a passionate Brexiteer yourself, did you have regrets? Did you reflect upon that information and then have regrets about how this was handled? Were there ways that the UK Government could have handled this rather more competently?

Lord Offord of Garvel : I do not recognise the premise here. The evidence does not back this up, I am afraid. The evidence is that we had a faster roll-out , and we came out of lockdown faster and our economy has not been damaged any worse than the European economy. I do not understand the premise of the question. I remind you of how angry the French and the Germans were that we had the vaccine deal sewn up months before they did.

Q88 Okay, but I think what the inquiry heard was that work that could have been devoted to planning for a pandemic was not possible because everyone had to plan for a no-deal Brexit. Surely that is the point.
Lord Offord of Garvel : The evidence does not bear that out.

Q89 Okay. T hank you. Getting on to error and fraud, I notice that the Public Accounts Committee recently came out talking about fraud and error, saying that total fraud and error across covid employment schemes delivered by HMRC was an estimated £4.5 billion, of which the Department expects to recoup just £1.1 billion . It criticised the length of time the Government were taking to recover those taxpayer pounds. Would you like to comment on that?
Lord Offord of Garvel : Is that the business fraud?
You are representing the UK Government.
Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes, the £4.5 billion. That is out of £146 billion of business support, so what does that work out at — less than 3% ?

Q90 It is about 4.6% apparently . I th i nk that is of the total ex pend ed in the three schemes — t he c oronavirus j ob r etention s cheme, the s elf- e mploy ment i ncome s upport s cheme and the e at o ut to h elp o ut scheme. Equivalent estimates—
Lord Offord of Garvel : Sorry, your percentage number was how much?
It is 4.6%.
Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes — less than 5%.
Q91 So is that acceptable?

Lord Offord of Garvel : It is not a case of being acceptable. It is a case of if you run a loan book — for example, if you are a bank and you have bad loans — you are in the same category, at less than 5%. I am not saying it is acceptable and you do not want it to happen, but that is within commercial margins of running a loan book. When you send money to people without them filling out any forms, and without doing any credit checks on them, I would say it is remarkable. The lesson of this is how remarkably honest the British people are.

Q92 But that is a considerable amount of money. What concerns is the Scotland Office raising with the UK Government about trying to claw some more of that money back? Is that something that is your responsibility as someone who is responsible for business?

Lord Offord of Garvel : Yes, there is a review of this going on, and it is within the Treasury as well, as they sent the money out. That is under review. It will also be considered in the covid inquiry.
Q93 Are you on top of it , though, Lord Offord?

Lord Offord of Garvel : Absolutely we are on top of it. A s I just indicated to you , overall that is within the realms of running a loan book in terms of a bad loan position at 5%. It tells you that in the main the money was well targeted, well received and being paid back. That is not to say it should not , therefore , be recovered where it can be.
Q94 That does not sound like you are pursuing it yourself. Is this something that concerns you? Y ou seem to accept it as a necessary result of h anding out that money as quickly as—

Lord Offord of Garvel : I do not reside in the Department whose responsibility it is to recover the money . T herefore , you need to inquire of that Department what precise steps it is taking to recover that money.

Q95 Does the Scotland Office, and you as the representative for business for the Scotland Office, ever feel concerned enough to contact the Department yourselves? For that matter, the Department for Health and Social Care apparently, according to the Public Accounts Committee, wasted an extraordinary £14.9 billion on PPE and related covid expenditure. W hat are you doing to tackle this?

Lord Offord of Garvel : Again, this is an unfortunate by-product of the speedy response that was required to save 15 million jobs, keep the population in employment and allow our economy to return. There are bad actors unfortunately in th is world that we live in, but the lessons that we are learning out of this is that the British people in general are very trustworthy, hardworking and honest people.
Q96 Of course, but clearly there were some problems here, so they presumably need to be addressed by the UK Government.

Lord Offord of Garvel : When was the last time you received a loan from a bank where it did not check that you could pay it back? It has never been done before. It is a most extraordinary experiment that we just undertook, to give money to people without working out first if we could get it back. Guess what? It has been returned.

Q97 Okay. Back in 2021 admittedly, looking at some of the spending measures made by SNP Ministers since the start of the covid -19 pandemic , the Scottish Government estimated fraud and error in those schemes to be no more than 1% to 2% of payments, which is approximately £16 million—
Sorry, I am being interrupted by Mr Ross.
I am just passing advice.
That was approximately £16 million to £32 million, which is a significantly lower amount. I do not have more up-to-date figures than that —

Order. I am finding it really difficult to concentrate because Mr Ross is constantly and consistently barking into my ear. Would you please be quiet and let Ms Brock ask her questions and the Minister res p ond to them?
I t seems that there was 1% to 2% fraud and error — [ Interruption. ] Do you know, it really is very difficult to ask questions when you are constantly interrupting, Mr Ross ?
Would you please stop interrupting?
I did not interrupt you. I was tempted, but I did not interrupt you.
I am not speaking to Ms Brock.
No, but you are speaking to the Chair and everyone else can hear you.

G etting back to that point, their estimate was something between 1% to 2% in terms of the schemes under discussion back in 2021. It just seems like a very high amount if it is around 4.5% lost to fraud and error. How do you explain that?
Lord Offord of Garvel : What are you trying to say? Are you trying to say that the Scots are lower or higher—
Q98 Were the Scottish Government more efficient in handing out that money than the UK Government? I am interested in your opinion on that.

Lord Offord of Garvel : I have not seen any numbers that demonstrate that Scotland was any different from the rest of the United Kingdom. All the numbers that I have inquired about are basically saying that we are in line —that Scotland is in line with the UK.

Q99 Good afternoon, Lord Offord. One of the challenges that was undoubtedly encountered with the distribution of these funds to businesses was the ability to administer sectoral support, because of a lack of information about exactly what activities businesses were engaged in. W hat lessons do you feel we can learn from the pandemic in terms of how we improve data collection in Scotland? Would there be a need, for instance, for a business register? Certainly, places such as Belgium have considerably more information on businesses. Do you think that would be helpful moving forward to properly understand what businesses are doing so that that support can be best targeted?

Lord Offord of Garvel : That is a fair question. I think in the UK we always strive to improve the data that we collect, and that will increase as we go more and more digital. We will be able to do that better. We must get the balance right between that and allowing people to maintain their privacy, but there is no question but that we want to get better at data collection and the Government do have the Office for National Statistics doing this. We do want to improve on that.

There are concepts of different schemes being discussed — about whether we have the business register for sectors and so on. We did hear some grumbling, for example, in the agricultural community about differences in how that was administered between England and Scotland. We did hear some differences around retail between Scotland and England. There were some differences employed and yes, on the face of it, if we had better data we would be able to drill down into that.
At the end of the day, we were in a pandemic. It was an emergency situation. We acted fast, and on balance it was a pretty good job.

Q100 I guess the obvious question then is : have there been any discussions that you are aware of within G overnment and between the Scottish Government and the UK Go v ernment as to what information it might be helpful to collect in future ? Is that something that has been discussed?

Lord Offord of Garvel : There are discussions going on. I know that certainly the Fraser of Allander Institute is looking at this and the Federation of Small Businesses has an opinion on this. It is an ongoing discussion.

Q101 We heard from the Federation of Small Businesses recently, and now that we have moved beyond the immediate health response of covid and businesses are still trying to get back on their feet, one of the things they were concerned about was the increased level of legislation coming from the Scottish Government to Scottish businesses. What discussion have you had with the business sector in Scotland about legislation? They particularly highlighted, for example, the d eposit r eturn s cheme , which obviously the UK Government have been involved in as well. Schemes like that, the w orkplace p arking l evy and such like are putting businesses off, particularly FSB members in their small business survey that came out. What do you hear from Scottish businesses about the level of legislation coming from the Scottish Government and how that is impacting their businesses?

Lord Offord of Garvel : I speak regularly with the Scottish business community, to stakeholders, and I do detect a frustration that they feel that they are in some ways having to deal with a greater amount of regulation. I think the word is “divergence”. Business does not appreciate additional regulation and divergence from the UK. The market is a UK market. They want a single market for Scotland— 6 0 % of our trade in Scotland is with the rest of the United Kingdom, 20% with Europe and 20% international.

Whether it is things like DRS, whether it is things like the gene - editing thing , which is technology invented in Scotland, in the James Hutton Institute , and being adopted everywhere in the UK except in Scotland, which seems slightly odd , or whether you have the issues around the proposed alcohol advertising bans and differences around rent freezes , the message I am getting is , “W hy is it different in Scotland ? Why are they putting up barriers? We want to trade across all the United Kingdom.” I get that a lot.

Q102 In some of these areas — for example DRS — we are told by the Scottish Government that the UK Government are disrespecting devolution by getting involved, but certainly what I hear from businesses is that they welcome the fact that one of Scotland’s G overnments — the UK Government— listened to the concerns of business over DRS and they are putting forward suggestions for a UK-wide scheme that they would be happy to work with. Do you agree with the SNP that it was disrespecting devolution ? O r do you agree with the businesses that it was vital for the UK Government to get involved and come forward to try to have a scheme that works across the whole of the UK?

Lord Offord of Garvel : The whole point of devolution is that devolution is a settlement within a concept that has existed for 350 years called the United Kingdom. The SNP Government are very familiar with the concept of a single market. They love the European single market, with 27 countries. They want to be part of that single market. What they do not seem to like so much is the concept of a UK single market. Yet for the UK to work properly we need a single market. The whole point of the UK Internal Market Act is basically to say that the presumption should be that in these islands we do everything the same unless there are legitimate reasons for exclusions, to which we set a high bar. Therefore, what the businesses are saying is that they are getting an increasing number of exclusions and diversions. The business community do not like that.

Q103 To follow up on that, waste management has been devolved for almost 25 years and the principle of devolution does allow difference. There was lots of difference when the UK, including Scotland , was in the EU and it did not seem to be a problem. The internal market in Europe allows exemptions for public health and the environment. Why does the internal UK market not allow that?

Lord Offord of Garvel : The issue with the DRS was simply because the product — the bottles — do es not respect borders. Having a scheme that works in one part and not in another part is fundamentally not working. T he Scottish business response was that certainly a lot of English suppliers would stop supplying the Scottish market—
The original plan was all four nations were planning to do glass.
Lord Offord of Garvel : I think that is where we come to—
It was the UK Government that changed.
Lord Offord of Garvel : I think that is where we got to , which is that w e want to do it together.

Q104 I asked the Prime Minister this in the Liaison Committee last week. Do the UK Go v ernment increasingly see their role as to correct and , if necessary, overrule the Scottish Government in schemes and measures that they do not like?
Lord Offord of Garvel : No, quite the opposite.
But you have. It has been done.

Lord Offord of Garvel : As p art of the generous settlement where money is sent from London to Edinburgh with no strings attached comes the responsibility of the Scottish Government to legislate within the rules of the devolution settlement. What the UK Government want the Scottish Government to do is to legislate legitimately within the generous devolution settlement , and we all will get along fine and work together on that. Where the UK Government must get involved is where the Scottish Government either goes across competence or puts a scheme in place that is to the detriment of the rest of the United Kingdom. At that point the UK Government have no choice but to intervene.

Q105 Can you explain why the UK Government changed their mind on glass, the most dangerous litter and one of the most recyclable materials? That is what changed. Scotland and Wales did not change from the start of all four nations planning to do the same thing.
Lord Offord of Garvel : In terms of the outcomes, where we have come out is to find a way that works for everyone in the UK. The best way to do that is to focus on plastics.
Q106 But you are not planning to do anything on glass?
Lord Offord of Garvel : That is going to be the UK scheme. The best way to deal with this is plastic. That is what the public want to see most : plastic recycling.
The last question is from Wendy Chamberlain.

Q107 There has been cross-party consensus on the need for a DR S and , as Dr Whitford said, across all four nations. One of the reasons given for the delay by the Scottish Government is the fact that we want to roll out on a UK basis. Are you confident that the UK Government are moving ahead in line with the timescales for DRS? Are we confident that the UK Government scheme is going to be delivered?
Lord Offord of Garvel : DEFRA is very committed to the whole recycling agenda , a bsolutely.
Q108 There is nothing that would suggest to you that it is not going to meet those timescales?
Lord Offord of Garvel : No.

We have knocked off at exactly 4 pm, which was the hour that we presumed we would have with the Minister . We are very grateful to you for coming along once again to this Committee. I think there were a couple of things that you said you might follow up on, if you could supply those to the Committee. I am sure your officials will have taken note. For today, thank you once again, Lord Offord, for helping us out in this inquiry.
