The Environmental Horticulture Group is a name that now fully reflects industry’s ability to provide solutions that can deliver across all 10 goals of the environmental improvement plan , and help tackle the climate biodiversity crisis and the transition to net zero.

There is a greater number of types of garden plant used directly by humans in the UK and globally than any other plant type. We use 50,000 types of food plants and 33,500 types of medicinal plants, yet the RHS Plant Finder lists 69,000 types of UK cultivated plants in this country. The RHS believes that there are roughly 400,000 types of garden plants. In comparison to the UK’s native flora, that consists of 1,500 types of plants.

For me as a plant biologist, all plants are brilliant, so we need to look after all of them and invest more in plant research and development, because they are so beneficial to humans. Some may be problematic, but the majority are beneficial.

Why is it that people use these cultivated plants? Results of an RHS /YouGov survey of the UK population in December 2022 revealed that 73% said that gardening had a positive impact on their mental health, 74% a positive impact on their physical health, and 42% a positive impact on their social health.

On behalf of industry, we would like to thank government for recognising during the Covid lockdown that cultivated plant diversity is as essential as food and medicines. That had a significant impact on improving the mental, physical and social health and well-being of this country, which has probably helped lessen the burden on the NHS.

I will also make a point on the changing climate. For example, a research paper that looks at several cities across the world and at the climate change models states that London will have a similar climate to Barcelona. It will not just be a climate similar to Barcelona ; it will also have significant frosts and significant drops in temperatures , so it will be Barcelona plus misery. This is why cultivated landscapes will become even more essential for tackling the climate and biodiversity crisis, particularly in urban areas, in addition to benefiting health. There are 700,000 [1] hectares of domestic garden in the UK; 49% of UK citizens actively garden , and 25% to 50% of urban environments consists of cultivated landscapes, so this is a huge area that has so much to offer in relation to dealing with some of these problems.

To be sobering, the most recent World Economic Forum global risks perception survey was published in January 2023. When we look at research, we are looking at between five and 10 years in relation to what could come out of this . The survey shows that the number one risk is failure to mitigate climate change; number two is failure of climate change adaptation; number three is natural disasters and extreme weather events; number four is biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse; number five is large-scale involuntary migration; and number six is natural resources crises.

Number one was climate action failure, so what I can say is that, with a decade or less in mind, the priority needs to be applied scientific research. That does not mean that the fundamental and the strategic should stop —t hey should be upped, with more investment in those as well — but we should be doing applied scientific research in real-world situations through a grow, test and learn approach, working with industry growers, landscapers, arboriculturists, gardeners and others towards providing sustainable, nature-based solutions that help tackle the climate and biodiversity crisis now and for the future, and improve the health and well-being of the nation.

For environmental horticulture research, we should also prioritise optimising cultivated plant genetic resources and cultivated landscapes, particularly in urban landscapes, to maximise climate resilience, adaptation and mitigation in order to benefit biodiversity, human health, and social and natural capital values, while remaining focused on the transition to net zero.

Focused research is also needed on minimising resource use and waste in the production of industry’s products and services , to maximise their environmental, biodiversity and human health benefits across the whole supply chain. The main priority themes of this research should be climate resilience , cultivated landscapes and plant adaptation, mitigation and resilience; biodiversity conservation and resilience, both cultivated and wild plant material; biosecurity and plant health; horticultural habitats for human mental, physical and social health ; and nature’s well-being.

These research priorities have already been worked up with industry and academia , alongside government, and are outlined on page 19 of the Environmental Horticulture Group’s Unlocking Green Growth: a Plan from the Ornamental Horticulture and Landscaping Industry , with work packages and work programme priorities. All we really need is support from the Government to make it financially viable for us to do this.

The economic outcomes and jobs for delivering this plan are also good. Key findings from the Growing a Green Economy report by Oxford Economics and Foresight Factory state that there are significant opportunities and benefits for the UK Government and the general public across several policy domains, which will provide economic growth linked to that plan, with the support of a sector that can grow to £41.8 billion in 2030, compared to £28.8 billion in 2019. This comes with a projected £8.7 billion UK tax revenue in 2030, up from £6.3 billion in 2019. The number of jobs across the country supported by the industry can also increase from 674,000 in 2019 to 763,000 in 2030, including in rural areas.

In effect, this is a no-brainer. All we need is support to deliver that plan. I also have a team of 10 universities and the horticultural industry and growers behind this, and we can just get on and do it.

Dr Lee Beniston : Good morning. I work for UK Research and Innovation, which is the UK’s largest public funder of research and innovation. Within UKRI , I work specifically for the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, where my role is to oversee the funding that we invest, with our partners, to ensure that businesses come up with a bioscience research base, which includes the horticulture sector.

I have a few points to cover on the first question . From a UKRI research and innovation funding perspective, we recognise the importance of the horticulture sector. It is important for me to say that we recognise that there are some long-standing research challenges and opportunities, as well as some emergent ones. These are not mutually exclusive and are applicable to both edible horticultural crops and ornamentals.

These are, as we see them in our portfolios, underpinning plant science and sustainable food production research, which is absolutely critical across the breadth of the horticultural sector, as we all know, specifically focused on the sustainable production of high-quality, nutritious food to meet the predicted increased demand in food by 2050 and beyond.

The s econd is research on climate resilience and climate-smart breeding, which we have heard a lot about already, but specifically with a focus on the development of crops that can tolerate, for example, heatwaves and periods of drought; that have different root architectures, such as longer roots, so that they can access available groundwater; and that can tolerate salinity and can be watered by brackish water where fresh water is in short supply. We also see research on reduced inputs overall—particularly water but also fertiliser—such as the development of crops that have improved water and nitrogen usage efficiency, including technological systems to inform irrigation strategies.

Next, we have a view on a research priority around pests and crop diseases. This is an increasing priority due to the loss of crop protection products, with the changes to regulation of agrochemicals, for example, increasing the demand for genetic resistance to pests and diseases in horticulture. Further, climate change is increasing the risks from invasive pasts, for which there is little native resistance.

Finally, there is a large category that we see as emergent around precision and controlled environmental horticulture and agriculture, specifically including robotics and automation technologies. Fundamentally, this encompasses a wide breadth of technologies. The committee has previously heard evidence on the precision application of fertilisers, the laser targeting of weeds, vertical farming, and aeroponics and hydroponics, which utilise UV lighting. Further examples include satellite applications for earth observation combined with sensing technologies, yield mapping for prediction, the targeting of inputs and selective harvesting, and the guidance of autonomous vehicles for cropping.

Q160 Thank you both. Lee, I would like to follow up from where you just finished , on the effectiveness of the structure around R&D and its delivery. It is a particular hobby - horse of mine, because I was responsible, with Harper Adams, for a report last November that looked at the efficiency of the application of science and the fact that our productivity levels in the UK have been lagging behind. Why is that? The conclusion we came to was that the whole structure is too fragmented. We have too many bodies and the relationships between them are not clear, so the flow of knowledge is not as effective as it should be. What is your view on all of that?

Dr Lee Beniston : UKRI is clearly a significant part of the R&D organisational landscape in the UK . W e would work with all partners across the research and innovation ecosystem for the full benefit of the breadth of the horticulture sector.

I can outline three main ways in which UKRI effectively serves the horticulture sector and others through our R&D operations and investment s . The first would be our open research and innovation programmes. These are responsive programmes, such as the BBSRC R esponsive M ode and Innovate UK SMART grant funding programmes. These are open competitions run several times a year, where funding is competitively awarded in response to opportunities identified by the research and innovation communities, including the full breadth of the horticulture sector.

Secondly, we also invest and partner across the research and innovation ecosystem to develop strategic research and innovation programmes. These are programmes that take a mixture of approaches, often in co-design, co-development and co-investment with businesses and other key stakeholders in sectors. They include specific programmes that we have developed to support the horticulture sector and other research and innovation communities.

The third main approach that we take, again working across the full breadth of the UK innovation ecosystem, is through our strategic engagement and collaboration activities. This is fundamentally where UKRI helps to catalyse and convene stakeholders in discussion and to support connectivity across key sectors, again enabling researchers to talk with businesses and other key stakeholders across sectors. For example, from a BBSRC perspective, we regularly attend crop conferences. In fact, we are a key sponsor with Innovate UK of Fruit Focus, which is forthcoming. We also establish working groups and strategic advisory structures across UKRI but also pulling from the breadth of the sector.
Finally, we work closely with government departments to understand the deployment of policy and how R&D should be guided in that regard.

Q161 F ollowing up from that, along the lines of Lord Curry, as an academic myself — I do not think that we have ever had BBSRC funding, so I do not need to declare that — the questions are very rarely led by the people on the ground : the farmers. How do you flip that on its head or turn it round? How do you get people who are dealing with these issues on the ground to lead the research questions? You do not get many farmers in a workshop, to be quite honest.

Dr Lee Beniston : I would address that through speaking about a couple of examples related to our strategic research and innovation programmes. They typically start with workshops. They also start with strategic scoping events and key meetings, where we will ask key stakeholders, such as farmers, processors and growers, and the whole sector what they see as the key research and innovation challenges. Typically, for the team I oversee at BBSRC, these are pre-competitive research and innovation challenges, where we are looking for businesses to work together to address shared barriers to innovation.

I point to one example , specifically in terms of farmers, processors and growers. The horticulture and potato initiative, which BBSRC invested in alongside NERC and the Scottish Government, included a range of 33 horticultural businesses, including farmers. That was an investment collectively of about £9.8 million and leveraged about £800,000 from the businesses and key stakeholders involved. That would be a good example of where we take things beyond workshops and aim to understand and structure strategic programmes around key needs in the sector.
Following on from the discussion in the previous session, how do you take that science and knowledge base and scale it up across the UK?

Dr Lee Beniston : We would work in partnership, for example, with Innovate UK to scale up. To cover a few key points, scale-up takes on various forms. For example, looking at awards through our responsive programmes, such as BBSRC R esponsive M ode , Innovate UK SMART , or, indeed, the strategic programmes I have outlined, we would hold key dissemination activities with partners in those strategic areas and discuss with them opportunities to seek follow-on funding. For example, BBSRC has a follow-on funding scheme.

We also work with Innovate UK to support enterprise skills, for example, to take that research further and scale it up. There is also the Innovate UK investor partnerships programme, and the UK Innovation and Science Seed Fund , which can attract really early stage, research-focused technologies through to seed stage and beyond, connecting through to investors. There are a range of ways that we do this.

We also have schemes such as the BBSRC LINK and industrial partnership award schemes, which enable businesses to partner with each other at an early stage or explore ideas that need to be taken further towards commercialisation. UKRI would support the breadth of the translation pathway.
You are giving us some very useful information, but it is at a speed that I am finding difficult to follow. I wonder whether we could slow down a bit so that I can take in what you are saying.

Q162 Before I ask my question, Alistair, I thank you and the RHS for the lovely invitation to Chelsea, which we very much enjoyed . How appropriate are current funding models for the horticultural sector?

Currently, the UK’s research and development funding streams and, indeed, policy goals, including the recently published environment plan in 2023, focus predominantly on funding earth systems, wild biodiversity in the natural environment and forests, or agricultural and food crops. They are really important and continue to need increased funding to support them, but that often leaves environmental horticultural funding opportunities as a bit of an orphan. Therefore, it is very difficult to access, leaving that funding for the environmental horticulture and cultivated landscape sector orphaned.

T o give you a bit of history and a picture in relation to funding for that, there was a report in 2018 called Securing the Future of the Garden and Horticulture Sector , which stated that the last 20 years’ investment in applied ornamental horticultural scientific research and development had decreased from £14.1 million in 1985 to £2.85 million per annum. The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (Amendment) Order 2022 marked the end of the AHDB’s levy work in the horticultural sector, particularly the ornamental sector, which led to an even further decline and the loss of further millions each year in R&D investment in the horticultural sector.

To give some recent examples of things that have been positive, water was mentioned this morning. Those funds for growers were very supportive and, in fact, take advantage of the UKRI’s knowledge transfer scheme, where we did a project on mains to rains in order to help the general public save water for the supply chain. However, o f the recent UKRI farming innovation fund winners announced in August 2022, 99% of that funding supported farming or food, and only one project — 1% — supported ornamental horticulture. Of the 13 successful projects awarded for the tree production innovation fund in 2022, only one was at the cultivar level, which will be critical in relation to climate resilience.

The other element is training and upskilling in relation to the infrastructure of support. We need to succession plan. I am getting older. We need younger scientists. We need to support and develop them. We need to put the “green” into green infrastructure. The problem and challenge that we face is that green skills are about energy efficiency, solar panels and air source heat pumps — nothing that is green. We can help deliver net zero and biodiversity net gain through that, because environmental horticulture provides green products and services. Therefore, this industry is not recognised by government , and this cultivated biodiversity is not recognised as part of the solution to deliver those goals.

By investing in that, the other advantage is that you can export consultants and get money that way. A very good example of that is James Hitchmough , who was involved in the Olympic Park. James Hitchmough is one of the best horticultural scientists in this country. I have worked with him on a number of projects. He exports his consultancy rates to China, Saudi Arabia and the USA on green infrastructure projects. Just imagine if we trained and developed, in the next five to 10 years, the next 10 to 15. The export potential of that expertise and knowledge would be gold dust, and we would be shown to be leading the way.

On the fragmentation of the industry, over the last 10 years in particular—I can talk only about the Environmental Horticulture Group—we have become a very strong collective voice, which is why the action plan is so important. We have worked bottom up, listening to what growers’ needs are, to understand the challenges and to directly put the research questions forward that will help them accelerate and increase economic growth.

Q163 Alistair, you heard what Dr Benison said about the myriad R&D schemes that are out there, and you provided a very comprehensive description of it. How do smaller growers and businesses access all those wonderful national schemes that we are hearing about this morning? There seems to be a bit of a disconnect with what the Government are doing nationally. You said that a lot of the grants do not go to the horticulture sector, but what is the barrier? What is the problem here? What can we do to make it easier to access some of that money?

There are several barriers. One is that we should be looking across. As part of the RHS , we have set up a hub and spoke model. The RHS has a £35 million investment in a research centre based at Wisley , and we have built a spoke model whereby we are working with 10 universities across the whole country that have the excellence, equipment and facilities in relation to those ambitions. The challenge faced there goes back to the perception of the environmental horticulture sector as less essential.

Both industry and government could work harder in relation to share , say, the water grant scheme with people and raise awareness of these funding streams . I tweet and go on LinkedIn to say , “ Hey growers, this is an amazing opportunity for you to improve that scheme”. As a micro - business or a medium -sized business, even for myself, scrolling across all the different research and innovation opportunities can be difficult, in that it is not linked to what the sector is offering. Some of the universities and other research academics in this country have teams that look at that as part of their business to make sure that they can be effective in it.

The current farming equipment and technology fund lists are heavily farm - focused . Although that is really important and should be supported, 92% of the equipment listed is for the agricultural forest sector , whereas only 8% is suitable for growers. It is about this suitability for micro-growers.

A Pye Tait report from 2019 talks about new technologies, automation and robotics, which are important and will play an essential part, but 55.5% of many industries are micro - businesses, 30.7% are small and 8.2% medium sized , and only 5.6% are large businesses . Across the industry, 94.4% did not expect automation, robotics or other technologies to be useful to their businesses.
Lee, you have heard from Alistair that he does not think that small businesses can access the R&D grants and so on. What is your answer to that? Do you have a strategy to help his sector out?

Dr Lee Beniston : If I may, I will also run through some numbers, but, on the point of access, Innovate UK’s smart responsive grant funding scheme is certainly open to small, medium and larger businesses. In terms of reducing access to that scheme, there is a sliding scale of what businesses are asked to contribute to those projects : t he smaller the business, the less it is asked to contribute.

Research council funding, for example, enables businesses to work with the research base and provides businesses with that early access to research knowledge and the ability to explore that. Again, I mentioned that we have our LINK and industrial partnership award ; other research councils have similar schemes. These schemes reduce barriers to access, because they allow businesses to provide in-kind funding rather than cash contributions, which we find certainly benefits small to medium-sized businesses. We strive to ensure that businesses of all sizes can access and collaborate on research and innovation funding.

On funding, I just wanted to provide some statistics by way of response to the previous question and as part of the access question. For BBSRC, horticulture, as I am sure you will know, sits within our strategic priority on agriculture and food security. On underpinning plant science research, BBSRC committed and invested £68 million per year in the previous two financial years—2021-22 through to 2022-23. Around £52 million of that investment related to crop science, and around £17 million per annum over those past two years related directly to horticulture.

We have heard some views on the Innovate UK-led programmes , in particular the Defra farming innovation programme and the transforming food production programme , in previous evidence, so I will provide some statistics on those as well. Again, on the access point, businesses of all sizes can access those programmes.

On the transforming food production programme, £22.8 million of funding was committed to 31 projects relating specifically to horticulture. On the Defra funding, which Innovate UK is delivering on the farming innovation platform, £14.2 million of funding was committed to 33 horticulture projects. Again, that is specifically to horticulture. It is important that I outline that there will be related projects, such as those on automation and technologies, which are more broad ly defin ed , but I just wanted to provide the committee with a snapshot. Across both those programme s , businesses of all sizes co-invested more than £18 million in those projects.
We might have to shorten some of the answers, because we are going to run out of time.

Q164 In terms of people being awarded grants and so on , in various ways, you have both quite rightly used words such as “adaptation”, “resilience” and “reduction of inputs” to talk about the response to climate change. We should also look at affordability. What questions do you ask before providing or responding to requests for funding? When you look at requests for grants, for example, do you think, “How is this going to support food security? Are we looking at something that is viable in this climate ? ” That is particularly in relation to edibles, as opposed to, for example, using a lot more water, because it might be a fruit that is not native to the UK.

Do you see what I am saying about diet and so on? Do you look at what people are trying to achieve, just so that we can understand better how those grants play out into outcomes that we can all enjoy?

Dr Lee Beniston : The open responsive programmes of grant funding would always seek to support and fund scientific excellence first and foremost. They are important for continuing our investment in long-term research capability. However, the strategic programmes that I have mentioned—particularly those that involve businesses and other key stakeholders in the sector—will be co-developed with businesses , which will often co-invest in them . On that basis, they have strategic challenges that are specific to whatever that group of stakeholders is looking at, such as reduced inputs.

We have a couple of examples. On bacterial plant diseases, which are applicable across the breadth of the horticulture sector, BBSRC, NERC, Defra and the Scottish Government invested around £13 million against a national priority that was focused on Xylella fastidiosa, a devastating plant pathogen that can cause incredible losses. That is a good example of a programme to deliver a national priority, where the research funded within that would be directed towards that.

There are many examples that we could give the committee but we certainly do both. It requires a balanced approach to ensure that long-term research capability , and a focus when we need to be agile and react to national needs and priorities.

Q165 How effectively are businesses incentivised to invest in R&D? I realise that this will probably fall into two sections, because grants are never 100%, so they will have to put some of their own money in as well. There may be other projects that are not supported by grants but businesses would like to invest in. I wonder whether businesses ’ investment in R&D in the horticulture sector has gone up or down in recent years. If it is down, how could we improve it? How could we incentivise them better? Do tax credits fall into this category, for example?

On the awareness and understanding of tax relief levels, there is a claim in research and development , but i f you look at the leading countries across the world, including Chile, they are giving significant percentages of tax relief to some of those aspects and making it easier, particularly if you have a consortium of growers. It tends to be that that tax relief has to benefit research but also be the thing that benefits wider research. If you have a consortium of growers, all of them should be able to get that tax relief because they are collectively working on something for wider horticulture, but it falls down in some respects because of that.

As touched on this morning, incentivisation is about this whole package. It is particularly around things such as transitioning to net zero. We need to look at how we reduce the risks of market failure and to think about things like water. It is about not only doing the R&D but putting the infrastructure in place and doing the training and skilling together. There is a collective package at the end of it, whereby you come out with that multiple level.

There are areas where investment has benefited. One example I can give is Melcourt composts, which is a peat-free, alternative, sustainable growing medi um , which has invested significantly, as have quite a number of others. It has grown significantly and almost doubled its profit margin over the past 10 years. It has been able to reinvest in that while dealing with some of the challenges there.

Those are the key areas of incentivisation. The water one is good, but again, it is not the whole package. It not R&D , the infrastructure , or the training and development. Having a package like that would be really helpful to incentivise that investment .

Q166 Going back to the potential withdrawal or not—no one is quite sure yet—from Horizon 2020, is that already having an impact or is it something that we are able to facilitate in other grants? Are there other ways around it?

Dr Lee Beniston : UKRI is pleased that the Windsor Framework allows the UK to progress discussion on association. A s you alluded to, the timing and process for association following the publication of the Windsor Framework is not yet certain, but we are monitoring events closely and working with DSIT on contingency plans if association is not possible. We absolutely recognise the importance of stable and sustained investment for our research and innovation communities, which includes horticulture . w e will continue to listen carefully to those communities, in particular their views on international collaboration.

It is important for me to say in response to this question that UK researchers and innovators can still apply to Horizon Europe. Eligible, evaluated and successful UK applications to Horizon Europe have access to the UK guarantee. Until agreement is reached, it is important that UK researchers continue to apply through the guarantee, which I believe has been extended to 30 June.

Could I push back slightly there? I agree that you can apply, and I sit on one of the Horizon 2020 panels, but one of the real problems is that UK people are now being excluded from the grant applications. Although you can apply, you cannot join in with the large consortium bids, which is where the real problems come in, because that is where we should be learning. I hope that we can look beyond just Horizon 2020 at other issues that are coming through. How do we develop that cross-country, cross-continent relationship in the UK?

Dr Lee Beniston : UKRI has supported extensive collaborations in the past , particularly in relation to horticulture internationally . It will continue to do that through working with its partners internationally as well as through government. I cannot provide a view on what may or may not happen.

I am not asking that. Thinking broadly beyond that, should we link it to trade deals that we are building with other countries? What is the way to rebuild those bridges in research? Right now, it is not clear how we will rebuild them. Have you any thoughts on that?

Dr Lee Beniston : As I say, we need to continue to invest in research capability for the long term, and that would, of course, include international collaboration. I cannot comment on government policy in terms of what we should or should not do.

I am not asking you to comment on government policy. Are there particular areas that we as a committee ought to be recommending that the Government look further at because there may be benefits to be had from them?

Dr Lee Beniston : I would go back to my statement in terms of the research priorities that we have identified. I suggest that they represent priority research and innovation focuses where the committee might wish to consider encouraging collaboration, particularly internationally.

For many leaders in the scientific community, Horizon Europe is critical. We have built up long-term relationships and friendships with communities and groups with which we can already run and share new developments. There is a real challenge to replicate the full benefits of the world’s largest existing collaborative research programme. It has readymade routes for talent, facilities, equipment, access and collaboration with those multiple countries. That is not to say that we should not build on that, because we absolutely should, and look to work with others. Looking at the finances of that, there is an estimate that it will be more than what we have given but, if you were to truly calculate the money that you are getting from the facilities, equipment, staff and all the others, it would be significantly less leverage of those aspects.

The other thing I would mention—of course I would—is that, although it is brilliant that we are looking for alternatives, the priorities in Pioneer are for green infrastructure, not plants. T hose key elements do not include the horticultural sector. We are emailing and having conversations to try to make sure that those things, particularly around cities and green infrastructures, are looked at in relation to research and development. There could be a lot of sharing, particularly with places such as Singapore.

Q167 You touched on the Government’s Pioneer programme , as opposed to Horizon. Horizon is a big beast internationally, not only in Europe. I went on a trade delegation to India, and even they were talking about Horizon and wanting to be associated with it. Now, of course, we have pulled out of the EU and the Government have this Pioneer programme, which the Government have called bold and ambitious , with billions of pounds of UK investment in global collaboration and more funding for UK research. How confident are you in the effectiveness of th is new programme? Will it be just as good, better or otherwise?

I t is hard to say from looking at the document . We need to work closely on its development, particularly around plant sciences , and environmental horticulture and farming. We need to be there and to have an understanding of what that will mean for existing collaborations and friendships, which often create very good outcomes and impacts. It is hard to say, but again, we need to make sure that green ing green infrastructure is high on the agenda within that aspect of support.

Dr Lee Beniston : The Government’s recent update on Pioneer includes a set of commitments that cover four key pillars of funding that long-term alternatives would deliver in addition to transitional agreements and third-country participation. They are global collaboration, infrastructure, innovation and talent. International collaboration is woven across all four Pioneer pillars, enabling UKRI to build and strengthen global partnerships that already exist, as well as creating opportunities for us to increase connectivity for the UK research and innovation ecosystem, and collaborations across the global research and innovation ecosystem.
On the green industrial growth, health, innovation and everything, you think it would be something good for the UK out of Europe?
Dr Lee Beniston : I cannot comment further on this.

Q168 Looking beyond what might or might not happen with these various projects, can you give any concrete examples now of other countries using really good R&D policies that have got results? Can we learn from them?

Dr Lee Beniston : UKRI would agree with evidence that this committee has previously received about looking towards the Netherlands, in particular Wageningen , which offers an excellent opportunity to learn in terms of R&D policy. That said, in previous evidence you also heard about the distributed nature of the UK horticulture sector. One might have to take a view as to whether the structure of policies , government levers and R&D funding around Wageningen is appropriate for the UK. We would need to consider the approach that it take s and how it do es it in terms of R&D policy, and then understand how that might relate to the UK horticulture system specifically. In terms of best practice, we would look to Wageningen.

If you look at impact on paper s , the top countries that are doing good horticultural science are China, Germany and Russia—all countries that are never really mentioned. Because horticultural science cuts across every policy area, we should lead the way, create the right model and show a good example. At the moment , if I look out there, Wageningen is not the right model. There is no right model.

That model should have R&D policy best practice. It should look at the industry, government and cross-disciplinary hub and spoke model that taps into the UK research infrastructure, equipment and facilities. It should have the ability to merge and have academics from economics, environment and social. It should directly deliver on industry challenges through communicating with the industry. Like I said, I do not believe that there is anywhere in the world that does this model well, and this provides us with an opportunity to lead the way.
Would you not include the United States in that list you gave of Russia, China and Germany?
There are significant challenges in the USA in relation to the climate adaptation and climate change responses we have to make in the next couple of decades.

Q169 I just have a supplementary that links back to earlier questions. Lee mentioned Wageningen in the Netherlands. Is there a gap in our structure that is inhibiting us from the adoption of science as effectively as we should be? I declare an interest. I was asked to look at this concept of a What Works centre as a potential way of translating science and making sure that it is readily available. Is there a gap in this structure?

Dr Lee Beniston : UKRI , specifically BBSRC, has worked closely with policy on structures such as the What Works centre model. In the dissemination of knowledge and policy, the key is to bring together key stakeholders in the sector in a strategic way around research-led innovation challenges, as I spoke about. That provides an opportunity within those programme structures to share and disseminate knowledge, which leads to informing policy at a national and strategy level. That is something we have been actively doing across our strategic programmes, which are directly relevant and of relevance to horticulture.
Is that recent?
Dr Lee Beniston : Yes. I can give some examples of programmes that I mean, but it is recent.
Q170 Chair, so inspired by Baroness Fookes have I been that I applied to join the RHS yesterday.
Thank you for supporting our science and our community work.

In that light, you make a compelling argument for a new R&D framework. You have obviously done a lot of work on this over many years. Can you help fast-track the committee’s thinking and tell us how much it would cost?
I would say between £10 million and £20 million.

Q171 I was just thinking about the horticulture sector in the UK, where margins of profitability are pretty narrow and there is considerable precarity in terms of businesses’ future viability and sustainability. Is that different from other countries? Does it inhibit those businesses’ ability to put in for grants where they have to provide 20% of the money themselves anyway? Is it different from other countries?
It definitely is for tax credits. Some places, such as Chile, offer 40% tax credit elements, and there are other incentives. There are countries that are doing significantly more on that.

The other area is investment in horticulture through banking systems and loans, because they see it as risky. I have painted a picture of the opportunity for a thriving industry. The opposite could equally happen if we do not support this industry through market failure of water, peat, plastics—all the things that it is challenged with—and particularly energy. Just recently, at least five nurseries that I am aware of have gone out of business because of energy.

Therefore, I am saying that this is an opportunity not only to grow and thrive but to make sure that the trees outside there that cool our cities, capture the pollution and give us well-being remain so that we have resilient landscapes for the whole of society. There are certainly examples from other countries that could be taken in relation to how they support and invest.

Dr Lee Beniston : UKRI continuously evaluate s its programmes to ensure that businesses can be part of them. A recent initiative focused on crop and pest diseases for UK agriculture and horticulture. That was a £2 million investment, where we worked with Defra and AHDB on the UK plant health risk register to identify key emergent diseases. For that in particular, we worked through research and evaluations that we had done with our previous programme s specifically focused on horticulture to understand how to further and more greatly enable businesses and key stakeholders to be part of our research and innovation programmes. We are continuously striving to understand that. Again, it is not just about quanta of funding.
Q172 I get to ask the last question. If there was one thing that you could ask from Government, what would it be?

To p rovide funding through the farming innovation funding or other available funding streams to deliver the plan for the industry in Unlocking Green Growth . That would help society as a whole, both in its health and through climate resilience and mitigation, with the added benefit of economic growth from a shift from £28 billion to £42 billion and an increase in jobs in this country.

Dr Lee Beniston : We encourage the Government to follow the S cience and T echnology Framework recently set out and published in March this year. Through the approaches and priorities set out in that, we would encourage that they continue to work with UKRI so that we can effectively work with stakeholders in the research and innovation ecosystem across the UK, in particular the horticulture industry.
T hank you very much for the work that you have put in and for coming to the committee . That is the end of the session.

Oral evidence: Child exploitation and county lines , HC 1114
Tuesday 4 July 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 4 July 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Mr Robin Walker (Chair); Caroline Ansell; Miriam Cates; Anna Firth; Nick Fletcher; Kim Johnson; Ian Mearns; Mohammad Yasin.
Questions 52 - 1 19
Witnesses
I : Bali Rodgers, Co-founder and Director, Refocus Project ; Lennox Rodgers, Co-founder and CEO, Refocus Project ; and Junior Smart OBE, Founder, St Giles Trust.

II : Commander Paul Brogden, Lead for Gangs and County Lines, National Police Chiefs ’ Council ; Jahnine Davis, Panel Member, Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel ; Mark Kerr, Deputy Chief Executive Officer, Children ’ s Homes Association ; and Simon Ford, Head of Community Safety, Southend-on-Sea City Council.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– [Add names of witnesses and hyperlink to submissions]
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Bali Rodgers, Lennox Rodgers and Junior Smart OBE.
[This evidence was taken by video conference]

Q52 This is the second session on child exploitation and county lines . T oday we will be hearing evidence from Bali Rodgers and Lennox Rodgers, the c o- founders and d irectors of the Refocus Project. You are very welcome. On the screen we have Junior Smart OBE, the f ounder of the St Giles Trust. Thank you for joining us. I will start by asking each of you to briefly outline the work of your organisations in this area and your own experience of the area. Perhaps I could start with Bali or Lennox Rodgers.

The Refocus Project is a crime prevention and intervention service. It has been going for the last 18 years. It was birthed from Lennox Rodgers ’ s experience of coming out of prison and being unable to get a job due to his past. Somewhere along the line we met and I helped him to develop Refocus and we continued the work, working with young people.

We have worked with outreach and one - to - one services. We have done school s prevention work and prison work. Primarily it is all about awareness and prevention, but we have worked with high-risk young people as well over the period of the last 18 years. It is sometimes commissioned , sometimes not. It is very charity - based and on the ground.
Q53 Lennox, can you say something about your experience in that and how it led you to want to help others?

Yes. When I came out of prison I was asked to talk to a local south-east London gang, which was committing all sorts of crimes, county lines and using weapons. I was asked to talk to them about my lived experiences and they sat and listened. There were about 40 of them. They sat and listened to me for about two hours and they were in shock. I looked at their faces and they just looked like little kids. I thought, “W ow, how can I encourage them not to walk down the same path as me? ” From there, Refocus was birthed after having a conversation with Bali about what I want to do for these kids. I said that I just want ed them to refocus their lives. Bali said, “Perhaps that is the name we should call the charity, Refocus”.

F rom that talk we managed to rescue a lot of young people who just wanted to come out of the gangs. They didn ’ t want it. They thought, “Wow, if that is what his experience is like, if that is what the consequences are like, we don ’ t want it , ” and so the gang started to disperse.

Q54 That is very impressive. Do you think that you would have had a hearing from that group of people if you had not been through what you had been through? That was presumably essential, your lived experience in that respect.

It would have been very difficult had I not been in two gangs myself, been through the care system, been kicked out of many schools and been sexually abused and raped, and the racism. If I hadn ’ t had some of those experiences, it would have been very difficult. From listening to my experiences, girls as well as boys volunteered information. The girls were sexually abused and raped in the gang and they were able to talk about it after I shared my lived experiences. Girls are a subject to do with county lines and gangs that is not talked about enough.
Q55 Thank you for that. Can I bring in Junior Smart at this point to talk about his organisation and his background in this as well, please?
Good morning to you all. Thank you for having me. I am very impressed by the work of Refocus. I happen to know of its work and have been an avid follower of its amazing work for quite some time.

My background is not too dissimilar to the young people we are trying to help. Similar to Refocus, I have that lived experience. Yes, unfortunately I was sent down in 2001 for a drug-related offence, for which I originally received 12 years, which was later knocked down to 10. Literally from day dot in custody I decided I would do as much as I could do to help other people who were caught up in the same situation as myself. My case was quite well documented. No legal team would even attend the police station, so I was at this place where I was like, “O kay, if there isn ’ t help for somebody like me, then there should be . ”

That led me to a journey of change that first started with the Samaritans. I became a prison listener. I was helping people who were struggling in coming to terms with their sentences. I then went on to do many different bits of work, one of which was mentoring young offenders over in Rochester Y oung O ffenders I nstitution shortly after there had been a riot. That brought me face to face with the reality of the lifestyle that I had been a part of.

The connection from there led me to St Giles Trust, which I have to say is an amazing charity. It is the sort of charity that would come into a prison and meet somebody like me, which it did. I was later given an opportunity to sit and interview at St Giles Trust six months before my release. I sat the interview and I got it. That job was to establish the first intervention around gangs using ex-offenders. Despite its disbelievers, people thinking that it was too risky and that it would not work, SOS, the project I developed, has gone on to reach thousands and thousands of young people and their families who have been caught up in this terrible situation that we have with young people and violence, peer - to - peer violence. I have spent close to the last 20 years of my life engaging , with the support of a massive team now. SOS is huge.

I also developed SOS+ in 2008. Back then we had record serious youth violence on the streets, numbers that are dwarfed by today ’ s standards, it has to be said. I developed the first school s intervention project, which does exactly that. It goes into schools, colleges and pupil referral units and for this last year alone we have reached over 90,000 young people through school sessions. We are imparting real tools to young people.

I agree completely with what the other witnesses have said. The reality is that young people do not have people they can talk to. I feel very sorry for young people. There is so much misinformation out there around what happens when you are carrying drugs, what the consequences are and what happens when you are stabbed. I have asked kids, “Is there a safe place to stab someone?” and on average around 90% of people will say, “Yes, there are safe places to stab”. That is the wrong narrative for them to have.

When they realise that we are the real deal, they start opening up and they ask questions that they could not ask of a teacher, a parent or anyone else, but that they are likely to ask of their friends. That is why I think that lived experience, as dark as it may be—I am sorry to hear about his experiences with all sorts of trauma and abuse, mine too —it is to realise that that lived experience does have value. I am sure that the Committee has heard from the police time and time again. They will say, “We cannot arrest our way out of this , ” but from the young people ’ s perspective, who can they trust? Who can they turn to? That is where people with lived experience have the edge and they should be included in the discussions because they know what the solutions are.

Q56 Trust is so important in this because you have young people who are looking to gangs sometimes to provide that support and authority that they do not get from elsewhere. Can each of the members of the panel talk a little about the main factors that you find draw people into county lines and gangs in general?

Having worked in Refocus for 18 years, we went on a mission to start working with children at a younger age. We talk about early help, but I am talking very early signs when they are in school and they are showing reasons why they don ’ t want to be going to classes or are falling out because of their behaviour. We did that intensely for 95 young people we worked with for two years. We picked up that the primary issues were money, which was a major issue, and domestic violence. I am talking at primary school transitioning just into secondary. These were the issues. They were getting into fights. They were learning their way of being able to defend themselves. They were falling out of class because they had neurodivergent issues that were not being addressed and they had not managed to get a diagnosis before they had moved into secondary school. Unfortunately, even if they had, they were not being managed or supported and the families were not being supported.

My expertise is that I am a counsellor myself. I have worked in therapeutic backgrounds for years. I have run rehabilitation centres for women and drug addictions so I was very much about wanting to address the issues at the root. The root is that the struggling family has no support and unless we develop wraparound support for them at the earliest stages—I am not talking when they have been excluded, I am talking before. Experts like us see what is about to happen and that narrative that is about to pan out for that young person. Even before they have been excluded is where we need to address the issues, not after. After is too late. Things have already become embedded. We can change behaviour before that stage. You can learn behaviour; you can unlearn behaviour, unless it is too late. There are too many benefits to not chang ing for the young person when they have gone far a way down the line to being drawn in.

That is my passion, which is why we have set up the Safer Communities Alliance, which is a sister organisation that I run. It is an umbrella organisation that captures the stuff that Refocus is not able to, which is to provide microwaves for leaving carers who cannot eat because they cannot afford the electricity. It provides clothes for their first month of employment. In partnership we are working on developing some of the underpinning things that are creating that environment where children end up involved in crime. We find that the families who are struggling the most are like the ones I said , around domestic violence, war-torn issues that are not being addressed, generational trauma that is coming over from not being addressed in school and not being addressed for the whole family.

What is missing in all this is that we are not looking at the family. We are just looking at that one child and trying to tick the box of what we have done when we have been given the funding to do it and that is it. What we are not looking at is that wraparound support, which is what the Safer Communities Alliance is doing now. I have been funded to develop that wraparound but on a small capacity. We cannot do that on large grants and big commissioning. It has to be localised. It has to be about developing local villages again and people looking out for each other.

The only way you are going to develop that culture is to encourage that localised support and encourage small organisations. I love St Giles Trust. We know Junior. The smaller organisations have the capacity to stick around for years. The larger ones not necessarily because of the pressures of the targets and the money to keep themselves as big as they are. I have done both, but personally I am going to—
You need that to really reach into a community.

Yes, and embed yourself , because the young people are there and that continuity for that young person is there when everything else has gone, funding has finished and targets are gone . T he service is still there. Whether we have been funded or not, we have stayed there.

Q57 I want to pick up your thoughts on this. In the last decade or so , 760 youth centres have been closed and 4,500 young people ’ s jobs have gone. One of the ways to keep these people away from falling into the wrong hands is to keep them busy. The youth centres are not there. They have nothing to do, especially after school. They fall into the wrong hands. Do you agree with that ?

Absolutely, 100% . In this report w e asked 10 of the young people that had been involved in county lines what they felt the solution was. One of them wasn ’ t the run-of-the-mill youth club, it was something that was engaging, something that they needed that was going to give them some optimism. They already had neurodivergent issues ; t hey had fallen out of education. They did not feel that they could pursue English and maths, so they had made the choice to slip out, and they are drawn into county lines. They felt that they needed something that was more engaging for them and relative to them.

The only way you are going to get that is if you listen to young people and let them be the ones to set this up. We have a young person we have employed who wants to develop music. He said the only way that children like to express themselves is through music. They want to express their trauma. Trying to set up something for music is a nightmare because it has to come under the umbrella of a youth hub and a youth club , but what does a youth club look like? We have to be where young people are at and develop things from where they are coming from rather than have our concept of what youth clubs should look like.

I have a comment that I was reading on the way here and it says, “Not the run-of-the-mill snooker club, snooker table and table tennis. We want somewhere where we can sit”. We have set up a forum of 16 to 25 - year-olds who sit there and say, “We would like a master class in how to set up a business. We would like a master class on how to develop a recruitment agency”. The perfect job for them, all entrepreneurial, so why don ’ t we tap into their skills and help them with it and meet them where they are at? That is what the alliance is trying to do.

Q58 Good morning, panel. Picking up on the question about wraparound care, we have seen vast amounts of money issued to the police for tackling county lines and a massive reduction in funding to local authorities and third - sector organisations. Do you think that there needs to be a rebalancing of that funding to ensure that there are those preventative and early intervention opportunities?

100%. We have families whose children we see because the families are struggling. They have little children and we are watching them grow up and pursue that lifestyle because they do not have the support with social services to manage those young people. Instead they are being put in care and the parents are being criminalised. The parents are being charged and sanctioned for not letting their kids into education. We need that support, communities on the ground that are always going to be there. We are talking about relationships. If you have a relationship with a young person and you continue to be there, they will continue to come. We need money.

There was quite a bit there. The lady just talked about policing. We have been fortunate to do work with the police and to work in partnership with the police in various areas. It is a bit of a paradigm. The officers on the ground, the ones that I have come across, they largely want to know what the solutions are. Like, “Jay, teach us, show us how to engage with these young people”. They appreciate that it is complex. They appreciate that it is not a quick fix.

However, culturally the frameworks they are working with are dated. Officers do not get promotions based upon how many community members they work with. They do not get commendations for how many young people they connect and engage with. They get commendations based upon the amount of arrests that they make. What this leads to on a frontline level, if we consider the debate that has been happening recently around stop and search, we have to appreciate that it is quite damaging. For the young people, it is quite a shameful experience and young people ’ s voices are rarely taken into account here. On the other hand, we expect the young people, when it comes to the likes of county lines and child criminal exploitation, to speak up and speak out about it.

You then have to ask yourself , “H ang on a second, who is coming up with these ideas? ” Because every single thing, even from John Pitts ’ s research back in 2008 where he was talking to the young people directly, they were saying, “We do not talk to the authorities. We do not trust them”. Young people are scared about what happens if they talk to the authorities because they will be deemed a grass. The fear of repercussions against young people and their families is very serious and it is very real to them. How do we go back to rebuilding that? I agree with Bali. This has to be about relationship building.

Another thing that has to be mentioned and that has not been mentioned so far is the role that social media platforms have played in the proliferation of these groups. The amount of excuses that we routinely hear from these social media platforms that their platforms are not being used; however, I can honestly say to you that I see serious incidents happening online practically every single day. This is the reason why young people ’ s voices should be in the room because they will tell you that every single platform is being used to promote violence, to promote what the gangs are doing and to groom individuals. We have seen every single social media platform being used to groom and recruit young people into, for example, financial exploitation, county lines exploitation and sexual exploitation . T he list goes on and on. Again, we are not seeing anything happen there around that.

What happens when young people have limited availability of choice — especially now where the cost of living crisis is so high — is that often young people say to me, “I hear what you ’ re saying, Jay . I know what the consequences are, but if I am doing what I am doing , m um doesn ’ t have to worry about where the rent is going to come from. Mum doesn ’ t have to cry. There will be less arguments in the house because there will be more food on the table. I can provide”. That is very uncompromising.

For many people, it is quite easy to say that this does not exist and we can vilify the parents. We can say to the parents, “The reason why you are in this situation is that you are not doing enough”. I put it to the entire Committee that there are some people who are not starting on the starting line with everybody else; they are miles behind. A quick example of that is right now there is a lady I am working with. There is violence happening in her community and she wants to move in order to keep her son safe. However, she has rent arrears and that means we have to deal with the rent arrears first. She has to be six months out of that before she can even consider bidding on another property offered by another council to move. That is six more months. In fact, we have to get her access to that money, which is often going to come from having to work longer, which means there will be less parental presence in the house. This is just one example. This is the reality of many of the families we are working with. It is not isolated to a small minority of the population. This is an increasing majority.

Can I bring in Nick Fletcher? I think what you said about exploitation online and through social media very much chimes with what we heard from our previous panel. That clearly is a matter of great concern to the Committee, so any more detail you can give on that will be welcome.

Q59 Thank you for coming today. It is good to see you. This is a subject that is very important to me. I run a role models programme, so I go into the prisons , but I also go into the schools and talk to young people and people who have already made some choices that have not turned out best for them.

With regard to interventions that prevent children entering this, you have spoken quite a bit about family and youth, but do you want to expand a little more on that, on what maybe we can do as Members of Parliament and what councils can do? What about parents? Do you get the chance to speak to parents? They are the ones who are right in front of the child, aren ’ t they?

There are two levels. You get the lower-level families that we have targeted over the winter period. The local authority funded us to do the warm hub approach. Because I work so closely with the crime prevention agency, which is Lennox and his team, we had his families that we targeted for those warm hubs. We managed to support a lot of them at an early stage with budgeting, housing issues, domestic violence, moving families from areas, trying to help them with their debts so they were allowed to move areas.

All that stuff is very hard for somebody like a service that is crime prevention because they are busy working with that young person. That is why we set up the alliance — because it focuses on the famil y, i t focuses on the siblings. We know that siblings play a key part in this because of learned behaviour once again. They are likely to follow if we do not capture them, so we try to capture them even younger. We are trying to put on programmes out of school, holiday clubs and activities, but we are saying to the schools, “Do not give us anybody but those who you know have ACEs, adverse childhood experiences”. We want those young people. We want them to feel that they belong. We want to develop a village for them so that they do not go down the same road as their peers.

You have to be working alongside services like Refocus and St Giles Trust if you want to do this. You cannot just set up family hubs. I know the family hub approach is very much the in thing at the moment, but our family hub is bespoke. It is bespoke because we are targeting the vulnerable families that are likely to go into — or their children are likely to go into — crime. The only way you are going to do that is partnership working with schools. Schools need a lot more education about what younger grooming and exploitation is because they cannot see the signs. Obviously lived experience workers can see the signs, so you go in and you are able to provide that education.

The other side of it is the police. We have talked about the police a lot , but the police really want to work with us. The problem is they change so regularly that the relationship they are building—we bring young people in deliberately on the day that we have our local beat there because we want to break down barriers with them, but they change. They are constantly changing. It does our head in. How do we develop it?

Continuity is key and the only way you get continuity is if you get long-term funding. We get six-month grants as a small service. What can you do and guarantee you are going to give a funder with six months? Eighteen years of evidence, which is what we are running on, is reputation, families dropping in, “I remember you years ago, Bali, in school. I need to speak to you”. Entrenching this provision into the community and having that localised service is key. I am singing from a different hymn sheet. Lennox probably has a lot of different things that he would like to say.

For me, some of these young people are badly out of control and the parents are at their wits ’ end. You can put things in place to help them while they are in the community but they are still at risk. You have to have places where you can almost, for want of a better term, deradicalise and unpick that negative behaviour. They need therapeutic help to tackle some of the traumas and issues that they have faced. They have to be there for a time. It needs to be a secure place so they are safe. It needs to be a place where you can teach them life skills, have a supermarket, a healthcare centre and education and training facilities. You have to have specialist psychologists and people who can deal with their type of trauma.

They can progress to get an education because they have had that help. You give them that college-type education where they are doing education part of the day and practical the other part. You get employers involved to offer them employment. In this complex place that helps them, you help them with housing. There will be places that some of the older young people can learn to live. They will have help to be able to manage in society. They will not be a target for the gangs because they will have a different mindset.

The cost of all this is not as much as what it costs for a child ’ s life. We are saving lives. I was part of a model like that in my youth and it worked. I am still part of a group of people who were in that model with me. We are on Facebook and we still talk about how things used to be, except that it was a bit stricter back then. I feel that we need to have these places. You can use this model to tackle mental health issues and addictions. If you invest in the right people and the surroundings where they can learn to live a better life, then it will go a long way in reducing county lines. A lot of gangs are investing money to make money, giving away stuff, and we need to invest in the young people. We need to invest more in their education.
Q60 Do you think that we should be investing more into families though? Do these county lines prey on broken families, on that child who does not have that stable home?
They have come from those backgrounds.
Yes, and if they see that you have a close-knit family, that you see m um and d ad together with that child, it is very difficult to break into that.

Young people , as they get older , will want to pay their fees for uni , so that is not about targeting vulnerable families, but we have to do both. You have to do the early and you have to do the later. Lennox is talking very much about rehabilitation for those who are embedded into that behaviour because that is what helped us, helped me, helped Lennox, and in a way probably helped Junior.

The common denominator is money. Everybody wants money. I talk to a lot of young people and r egardless of their backgrounds that is what it is about. There is always a demand for drugs. Drug users are using the drugs to help cope with life, among other reasons.
It is a major issue.

Q61 Are we glamorising it in media and TV? Are we glamorising gangs? I have said this before and it has not gone down very well, but I genuinely do believe that what young people see on TV they want to follow and that is a huge influence on their lives. Do you agree with that?
I can see Junior is waving from the screen, so we must let him in. That is the problem with being on screen when we have other people in the room, but do come in.

I definitely agree with the last commentator. I think we are in a negative space at the moment where I would not call it necessarily gangs, but I would call it the criminal activity is being glamorised. We see this as a ripple effect. I agree with Bali and Refocus on this. What is the underlying need here? The underlying need here is money. The reason we have failed is that social media has given people a means where they can generate income by posting the most shocking and harmful content.

I am not going to mention any names because I think these people have had enough airtime already, but if you see some of the proliferators of some of the content their argument is always, “Well, the social media platform is there. I know that if I post content of me harming someone or threatening someone, I am going to get more views and therefore I can generate income” , but why do they need that money? They need that money because they need to make money to get out of where they are. I want to bring it back. The reality is that I have never worked with any young person who has not had goals. They all want the house and the car. They all want to see themselves as the boss. They want to see themselves as in control, but they lack the means to achieve that.

It is a dangerous narrative that we always say these things are missing from the family home. If you look at all the recent reports from Rescue and Response—and St Giles Trust is a part of that amazing service, engaging with people who are involved in county lines— you see that these groups are focusing on people who come from dual - parent households. One young kid I was working with, the mum is a researcher and the dad is a carpenter. He gets two holidays of his choice a year. How did he get groomed? How did he get pulled into it? What were the spaces?

If I was working with a young person and I said to that person, “Show me your time. What are you doing with your time?” I would be able to tell very quickly the likelihood of them being recruited or drawn in. That leads back to an earlier argument we had about where the young people go, where young people associate. I was visiting a youth club a couple of weeks ago where 90-something children showed up on that one night alone. The question is: if that youth club was not there , where would those kids be? They would be online, perhaps in the carpark, they might be hanging around on the street and that is only going to lead them to a situation where they may get stopped and searched. They may become criminalised as a result of that. This is one of the things that St Giles does so well. We have always engaged with the young people and their families. It is that joined-up approach.

The parents are often presented with situations that they do not understand — for example, an online repertoire and the risks that come with that. Often you might have a parent thinking their son or daughter is safe and the reality is far from that. A big question is asking parents out there, “What is contextualised safeguarding?” Most parents would not have a clue, but from a practitioner perspective that is absolutely everything. Where does that young person feel safe , and not just safe now, but safe at different times of the day? That just shows how much of a lack of awareness and understanding there is within the space. That is something again when we go into schools and we are talking to parents in the sessions . I think there is a gap between what knowledge is there and what knowledge is widely understood.

Q62 Thank you for that. I have one more , then we must move on. Sorry to rush you. What interventions work to best help young people once they have become part of an organised crime gang? How do you get them out?
That is the high-risk point.

It is very hard to get a young person out. They must want to come out. If they do not want to come out, then you are going to be working against the wind. If they want to come out, they must cut themselves off from all the social media. Sometimes it is very difficult because they must stay in the same area. What I have to do in my line of work is empower the young people to cope in difficult situations, whether it be coming out of a gang, living in a home where there are negative influences , or be in that school, having all sorts of issues with no help available. How do you cope when you are in a situation such as that?

I teach them how to cope in very difficult circumstances. Coming out of a gang there is not a one size fits all. Just to draw a distinction, there are county line gangs , but there are also groups of friends who do county lines or just sell drugs. Some of them are not targeting children. To get a young person out of a gang is very hard. You must work with them a few times a week and work with the families and guide them down a particular process , depending on their situation. Sometimes they may have to move.

Covid was a perfect opportunity. Some of the people we helped had to say , “H e is not around because he has Covid ” . Their friends can be trapped by some of these gangs and you must help them make a lot of changes, but it is very hard. Everyone ’ s situation is different. You need people who have been there and done it to help guide them along. Apart from the families and young people who need help and support , we need help and support to continue to do the wonderful work that our services are doing.

The amount of work that goes into it, I will give you an example . Lennox has spent probably one month helping a young person who came out of prison who was very keen to change. We babysat him in our offices, we made sure he stayed with us everywhere he went until we managed to get him somewhere where someone was prepared to take him into employment. That took four weeks. Lennox walked into God knows how many shops or places before he found someone that was prepared to take him on. All that extra work that goes into that one person is not just the amount of money that we have been given for that one person ; it is all the cost recovery, the investment that we have put in, night and day, to that particular person to rehabilitate their life. It is all the extras that are not considered. That is why if you have that continuity it becomes part of a culture that young people feel that they belong to and that they can continue to come to.

We have had about 25 young people in the last three years turn up on our doorstep because once upon a time I was counselling them in school when they were 11 and four or five years later they have sought us out. They have even contacted us from prisons and school, “Anybody know Lennox or Bali? Anybody know Refocus?” and they have turned up on our doorstep and said, “It is time for change. I want to change now” . How would that happen if a service is given funding one minute and they are gone the next? Who would they go to?
Junior, I know you want to come in, but I am going to let Ian ask his question because I think this is pertinent.

Q63 I think it is absolutely pertinent because it is about security of funding . H ow are organisations such as St Giles and Refocus funded and is the funding secure and sustained ? D o you feel there is a case for investing more in organisations such as yours? I am sure that you do.
Yes, 100%. I think it is more about the fact that you can—
I will bring Junior in first.
Sorry.

I agree 100%. I personally would like to know who is doing the sums that are saying X, Y and Z is how much is needed in this space . The ideology around the amount of funding compared to the need is just unbelievably low. You cannot even touch the sides. How many different reports have been done around county lines ? T o be honest , nobody knows how many young people are involved. The reality for us at St Giles is to create change . L et me just say this : across our county lines child criminal exploitation services we have been very fortunate. We have been able to see around 70% of those that we have worked with be able to engage, leave and potentially exit the exploitative groups that they are in.

Here is the truth of the matter: that work takes hundreds of hours to do. It is not a conversation. It is not something that can be delivered over lunchtime. It is not even something that can be delivered an hour every month for a year. This is intensive work. Anyone who knows the reality of working with these young people knows that the static factors, the dynamic factors, the threats to the home, the threats to the siblings — this is not just me saying it , t his has been evidenced by report after report —i t takes funding to do it.
Q64 Junior, I know there is not enough, but what I want to know is where does it come from? Where does your funding come from and how sustainable is it?

The reality is the funding that is out there is largely reactive. We can compete for funding pots. We are still largely dependent on a lot of donations. I think a lot of the institutions have woken up to the fact that they cannot address this by themselves. The reality is that it leaves organisations competing over funding to deliver work. What that removes from it is the creativity part of it.

One of the great things that we were able to do at St Giles is look at custody suite work. When kids are arrested and drugs are seized, that is going to create a drug debt. That is going to have consequences and repercussions on that young person and their family.
Q65 What proportion of your funding comes from public funds and what comes from charitable donations?

This is something we need to check, but I think the larger amount of money comes from the public purse in terms of the work around it. In terms of donations , there would not be enough there to meet the demand, although we are absolutely grateful for any donations we get.
Q66 It sounds as though you are bidding against pots of money all the time in order to sustain yourself.

Exactly , t his is the crazy thing. You might have an organisation such as Refocus competing against a larger organisation. You have heard it. It does terrific work, but there is not the money there to upscale and replicate that work . It is the same thing for St Giles. We are in a competitive situation, when what you need in that space is organisations working together because you need that space. My biggest concern is always the phone calls that I get from the families that are outside of the areas that we are funded to do the work in.
