Q371 Complicated. Is the Bill explicit enough in whether it underlines your intention to give public service broadcasters appropriate prominence when it comes to the user interface across the major routes — things like homepages, voice searches and that sort of thing?

Precisely how you deliver appropriate prominence will be for Ofcom to, first, produce guidance on . Ofcom will be tasked with going away and setting it out in rather greater detail than the Bill requires. Having set out the guidance, it will be for Ofcom to judge whether it has been achieved by the services that are designated under the new regime.
Q372 Is it appropriate that Ofcom has had to set out the specific steps that platforms should take to comply , or should they have been allowed to take a principles-based approach to this?

It is a judgment in that it will be for Ofcom to set out the guidelines, but to some extent it will be for the platforms to then decide how to meet those. If they get it wrong, Ofcom will tell them. There is a degree of flexibility — certainly an intention for a degree of flexibility— as to how they meet the requirements.

Q373 One other issue that has come up quite a lot over our evidence sessions over the last few weeks is the devices that are in scope of the legislation that you will be aware of. What kind of consideration did you give to including other multiuse devices like mobile phones and tablets, for example, in the legislation? Why did you rule them out?

It is designed to cover devices that people use predominantly for accessing television, which does not necessarily include mobile phones, for instance. There will be a determined list of regulated TV platforms and that is amendable if viewing habits should change. It is important in this area, as in so many others, that there is a degree of flexibility because we are in a world that is moving quickly. It might well be that people start watching television through pairs of glasses, for instance, in due course and the legislation needs to be able to take account of that, but at the moment, we are clear that it will apply to devices that are essentially marketed for the watching of TV content.
Q374 What about legacy platforms? That has also come up as an issue of concern.

You cannot require prominence on platforms that do not allow you to have it. If that is a problem, we can amend the legislation. Certainly we are sympathetic. That is not our intention at all and so we would listen to those concerns.
From what we heard, if you can clarify that in the legislation, it would be a definite—
If I may, it is definitely not our intention for devices that are no longer available or that can no longer be updated to be within the scope of this. We certainly will look at that again.

Q375 Can I move on to the “must offer, must carry” agreement? It slightly feels to me like an extremely elegant piece of Whitehall drafting that might not survive contact with the real world. You will have seen some of the objections. What is the aim of it? What are you trying to achieve?

The aim is to encourage the platforms and the broadcasters to reach a commercially satisfactory deal. We would not want to have to step in but the requirement that platforms must carry the PSB channels underlies that. That is part of the prominence agreement. Ideally, there should still be a net zero payment, as there is at the moment. You have sitting behind the negotiation between the platforms and the broadcasters the Government’s declared intention. We have called it “agreement objectives”, but it means that Ofcom is there to arbitrate if one side or the other complains that they are having unfair terms imposed.
Q376 Will Ofcom in the end be the backstop to set the terms of a commercial agreement between two private companies?

No, Ofcom is there to step in if one side of the negotiation is exploiting its powerful position against the other. It is more of a fair competition requirement than a Government-determined outcome, but it is a safeguard.

Q377 I talked about contact with reality. It is public that in Amazon’s new terms that come in in September for all advertising-based PSBs as well—everyone—it basically takes 30% off the top and that is it. When Amazon was in front of us, it said, “We have bespoke agreements with broadcasters , ” but, as I say, these are new terms coming out. We have had representations from PSBs saying, “Hang on, that is unacceptable . ” What would happen in those circumstances? Would Ofcom step in?

First, Ofcom will set out in due course more detail about precisely how it sees the negotiation being carried out and what it regards as fair terms. If your broadcaster felt that the terms imposed by Amazon were punitive and unfair, yes, it could go to Ofcom.

Q378 In practice, if Amazon says, "Tough", it will be forced to carry that —or , indeed , if one of the platforms says, “Hang on. We have to give away too much data or something to the broadcaster” . T his , in all other circumstances would be a normal commercial negotiation between, quite often, people who are big and ugly enough to look after themselves. I am interested that you think Ofcom will—

I do not foresee Ofcom having to step in in most circumstances. It is there as a backstop. For instance, when we have talked to platforms, they have occasionally expressed concern that they might be held to ransom by the fact that they have to carry a broadcaster but they are forced to do so under terms that they regard as unfair. The agreement objectives requirement is to ensure that this is a fair negotiation and that the outcome is fair. That has been achieved until now without Ofcom having that additional power and I hope that it will continue to be achieved without Ofcom using the power, but it is a safeguard.

Q379 Moving on to Channel 4 and the sustainability duty, I am slightly puzzled as to what that adds to its existing duties. The directors have, under the Companies Act legislation, a general duty to run a sustainable business. What is new in this?
You are right to the extent that I expect competent directors to take account of sustainability in decisions they make, but—
The law requires them to. You do not have to expect it.

No, because Channel 4 is not a company and so it is not covered by the Companies Act. You are right that a sensible director will take that into account. It is not at the moment set down as a duty of a director of Channel 4. We felt that it was sensible that it should be.

Q380 The big change is the removal of the publisher-broadcaster model. Do you have any idea of how the percentage of independent production at Channel 4 will end up commissioning , or do you have ceilings and floors?

Not at the moment. First, it is entirely up to Channel 4. We will not say that it has to have a minimum of in-house production. It could have zero in-house production if it wanted to have zero in-house production. This is a freedom. It does not mean you need to exercise the freedom.

We have been concerned about the dependence of Channel 4 on advertising revenue and its inability to diversify in the way that ITV has been so successful in diversifying its revenue base. This gives it the opportunity to do so.

We are looking at the question of whether the indie quota should be increased or precisely how it should operate. We will be talking to Channel 4 about that and it will in due course be set down. This is a basic freedom that Channel 4 has not had to date. We felt it would be of benefit to Channel 4 to have if it chose to use it.
Q381 Have you considered what the effect is likely to be on the indie sector? Will it mean more consolidation?

I am seeing John McVay later and no doubt he will give me his views on that. We are looking at the question around what the independent production quotas should be. Of course, that applies to qualifying indies. There are then the non-qualifying indies as well. We will set those in due course.

If I may, we absolutely recognise the point that you make and that it is important in this to engage with all the interested parties. We are trying to enhance the longer-term sustainability of the Channel 4 corporation while at the same time recognising the amazing work that Channel 4 has done over time in the independent production sector. We have been engaging with all those people from qualifying independents, the non-qualifiers and Channel 4 itself to try to strike the right balance.

It is also worth pointing out of course that many of the independent production companies with whom Channel 4 works have grown to be very big, which is a reflection of the success of the model, but we have to take that into account when calibrating this. It is not our intention to introduce excessively negative distortions. We try to strike an appropriate balance here, given the multiple objectives that we are targeting.
Q382 A previous Secretary of State thought that Channel 4 was unsustainable being left under the current model. Do you have any worries about Channel 4’s future sustainability?

Yes, which is one of the reasons why we are trying to strengthen Channel 4 by giving it the opportunity to diversify its revenue. Channel 4 is a small player in a world of big players and it has done remarkably well, particularly in recent years. We know that the climate at the moment is a lot tougher than it has been. Channel 4’s report is due out quite shortly but that will reflect the pressures that all commercial broadcasters are under at the moment. This is a changing world. We seek to give Channel 4 as much support to survive and thrive in the longer term as we can, but no doubt it will be tough.
Q383 I have heard from production companies that Channel 4 has suspended all commissioning over the summer, which has never happened before. Is Channel 4 under more threat now that it ever has been?

I have both seen those reports and talked to Channel 4 about them. Yes, that is a reflection of the difficult climate it now operates in. The advertising market has dropped considerably and that impacts on Channel 4 , particularly because Channel 4 is totally dependent on the revenue from advertising. Channel 4 will tell you that it is only a small number of productions and that it remains confident, but it would not conceal the fact that it is operating in a challenging climate at the moment.
Q384 Is that a case for cracking on with this? If this is the cavalry coming to the rescue, it had better come to the rescue—

This is a not a silver bullet. It will not suddenly remove the pressures that have been created by an adverse advertising climate, but it is an additional freedom. It is up to Channel 4 regarding the extent to which it takes advantage of it. It is entirely a matter for them. We hope that will help to sustain it.
Q385 Carrying on from Channel 4, it needs to at least sustain the level of activities over the long term. What do you regard as the long term in that?

The requirement is for Channel 4 to not take short-term decisions but to take into account the implications and it is not blowing all the reserves in the first year. It is a long-term sustainability consideration. As Mr Green was saying, in a sense, it is what any sensible director would be doing anyway. Putting this requirement into legislation will not change behaviour particularly because I hope that they were doing that already.
Q386 Is long term in the next couple of years, in the next five years, in the next 10 years? Do you envisage a time in the future when—
I would not put a figure on long term. We would not think of a particular figure.

We want the corporation and everything it does to thrive for as long as possible but recognising the challenges that the Minister has outlined. We are trying to focus minds to ensure that the issue of sustainability is as prominent for the board of the corporation as is delivering its remit. We believe that the two can go and need to go hand in hand.

Q387 Given those sustainability problems that Damian has outlined, and they are significant, Channel 4 at one stage was going to be a much bigger part of this Bill and a much more contentious Bill we all agree it would have been in that case. Genuinely, does Channel 4 have a future within this model? Are we looking at a massive taxpayer bailout in the years to come?

The last time I appeared before this Committee—and a couple of M embers here were present at that time—we had that discussion and at that time I expressed concern about the long-term sustainability. In a sense, the reasons why I expressed those concerns have not gone away. We decided not to proceed with privatisation but we, nevertheless, felt that it was necessary to take measures to try to bolster the sustainability of Channel 4, which is precisely why we give it this additional freedom.

Yes, Channel 4 is operating in a different world to the one in which it was created and it is, in international terms, a small player. It has done remarkably well. I hope that it will continue to do so.
Q388 If you were a betting man, what would you say is the percentage chance that we are staring down the barrel of a taxpayer bailout of Channel 4 in the future?
I am no longer responsible for gambling and so I will resist the opportunity to lay odds on it.

Channel 4 has been a remarkable success story. Everybody would agree with that. It has a strong management team. Again, probably members of the Committee will remember a few years ago under a different leadership when Channel 4 came and said, “The Government have to come and bail us out because we cannot survive . ” We did not and Channel 4 did survive. Now it is apparent that that was unjustified alarm, but that does not change the position. I am sure that Channel 4 will seek international deals. It will seek to take advantage in due course if opportunities arise with the new freedoms. I hope it will survive and thrive.
Q389 Do you think it will survive without a taxpayer bailout?
I certainly hope so. The Government would not like the idea of having to step in and provide taxpayers’ money.

The purpose of the Bill in its current form is to give the tools to Channel 4 to ensure that it does. Its current strategy sets out its plans until 2025. The board will need to consider how it wishes to make use of the flexibilities afforded by the Bill to set out its strategy to continue performing. Then it will be for everyone, including the regulator, to assess how well it is doing.

Q390 Good morning, gentlemen. Thank you for joining us. Sir John, you said just now that you had concerns about Channel 4 previously when you appeared before the Committee, but you expressed it rather more strongly than concerns. You said that without privatisation Channel 4 would not have the money to invest in future technology and programming. If you were right then, Channel 4 is now doomed, or were you wrong?

I was right to the extent that it had to make substantial reductions in its programming budget. We are not going down that road, but one of the reasons why we looked at the possibility was to give Channel 4 access to more capital to invest. There is an opportunity for Channel 4 to borrow and we believe and hope that Channel 4 can thrive without a rich owner standing behind it. Instead, it has the Government, which is certainly not rich at the moment, standing behind it. I hope very much that it will, but I do not retract what I said. It was an alternative way of bolstering Channel 4 potentially—

Q391 But you expressed your views in such strong terms. We all understand collective government responsibility. You hate this concession that you have made. Ever since I first met you, you were desperate to privatise Channel 4, desperate—
Mr Nicolson, I was not desperate. If you look at what I said last time I was here, I also said that no decision has been taken and that we were looking at it. We were looking at it.

Q392 I remember that famous picture of you when you appeared before the Committee and said, “We are not thinking about Channel 4 privatisation”. Lo and behold, you were photographed by a clever photographer going down Downing Street with a dossier under your arm about the privatisation of Channel 4, which we were led to believe your team had suddenly written inside about 36 hours—

If I can correct you, it was not me who was photographed. It was actually, I believe, a Cabinet Office official who was carrying a document that did set out that that was an option. As I said at the time—and we are talking now about five or six years ago—no decision had been taken and no decision was taken because it was not proceeded with then.
I stand corrected on that detail. It is a bit like the—
It is quite an important detail.
None the less, it was your Department. You know—
Actually, no, it was not even my Department. It was, as I said, the Cabinet Office.

Q393 I stand doubly corrected. It is a bit like the “Rocky Horror Picture Show”. We have been doing this so long that I feel we all know each other’s lines in all this. I can almost chant the lines that are forthcoming. None the less, Ernst & Young research for Channel 4 showed that removing Channel 4’s unique publisher-broadcaster model would result in a £2 billion reduction in its contribution to the creative economy over 10 years. That is worrying, is it not?
I am not sure I accept that analysis. Channel 4 will continue to commission programming. If it chose to do it in-house, that does not mean it suddenly stops contributing to the creative economy.
But it has said it does not want to do it.
Channel 4 said that it does not want to do it or it does not have to do it?

Q394 Is it quite a bizarre idea that Channel 4 says it does not want to do something and it does not want it in the legislation, but you will put something that it does not want into the legislation that it then says it will not use . What a total waste of time.

I do not see it that way. Channel 4 has not actively said, “Please do not put this in”. It has not told us that it would definitely use it, but giving them that additional freedom, particularly when we do not know the way the market will evolve in the future—and if we are to do it, we have to do it now because it will be a long time before another opportunity arises—seems to me only sensible. As I say, there is absolutely no compulsion on Channel 4 to start commissioning from within unless that is what it chooses to do.

Q395 Is the truth, Sir John, that this is a bit of fig leaf? You wanted to privatise Channel 4. Channel 4 fought off for a second time your privatisation plans. You did not want to exercise a full-scale retreat for a second time and so you said, “Okay, Channel 4, we will say that due to the pressure we put on you, we will now change the model slightly . ” It kind of went along with it and it looked as if all this wasted time actually achieved something when we all know that it achieved absolutely nothing , but it cost us, the public, quite a lot of money for you to go down this route again that you have retreated from.

We recognise and continue to recognise that Channel 4 will find it difficult moving forward unless changes are made. One of the options that certainly we looked at was privatisation in part or in its entirety. We decided that because that raised a lot of objections, which you know and which you echoed at the time, we decided not to proceed down that road, but that did not remove the concern about long-term sustainability and so we sought to address that through other means, which the Bill now does.
Q396 Before you go on, can I double check on the Channel 4 issue, John? What would be the consequences if Channel 4 does meet the sustainability clause? Would privatisation be back on the table?

Look, if Channel 4 is unable to sustain itself, which presumably is what you mean, it would need to come and talk to the Government about the consequences. It might come and say, “You have to bail us out , ” or, “We could look for alternatives , ” but that is hypothetical. I hope it will not arise. As I have said, strangely enough, it did arise a few years ago when that exact forecast was made by the management of Channel 4, but as it turned out it got through that period.

Q397 Quickly on STV, we have all had a meeting—and to follow up on the points that Mr Green was making—with STV. It is worried about Amazon. It is not pretending to be worried. It is worried. Amazon is a thug. To go to a relatively small company like that and say, “Unless you hand over huge amounts of your income, we will not put you on our platform , ” is a thuggish way to behave. It has enormous power. STV is worried—there is no secret about this—that it will not be able to resist. What advice would you give to STV?

The advice I will give is that help is on its way because that is the purpose of this Bill. At the moment, there is not the ability to bring in Ofcom if STV feels that it is forced into punitive terms by—I am not sure I agree with you about “thug”—a large company like Amazon. Under the provisions of the Bill, it will now be able to appeal to Ofcom and Ofcom will have the power to step in and judge whether these are fair terms.

Q398 One of the problems that STV identified is that a number of different companies are all subjected to the same technique by Amazon. When Amazon appeared before us, it suggested that there might be tailored negotiations and tailored agreements, but STV does not know what agreements other companies are having. This is an example where good old-fashioned trade unionism kicks in. If all those smaller companies got together and disclosed what Amazon was saying to each of them, maybe collectively they could fight off Amazon or at least get better terms.
The terms are bound to be commercially confidential between the individual companies—
That is of course what Amazon is saying and what STV is saying as well, but that commercial confidentiality goes against STV’s interests. It has absolutely no idea what deals Amazon is doing.
Ofcom as a regulator is there to assess whether the terms are fair and would take into account the behaviour of Amazon in its general negotiating approach with different companies.

To be clear, if you step back and look at the process that the Bill provides, Ofcom will have to prepare a code of practice to help support the approach to the agreement objectives. In section 362AK in the draft Bill, it has to consult on that. Both parties involved can submit their thoughts. That will then provide a framework to guide those negotiations, which, as the Minister said, we intend to be commercial negotiations and effective negotiations.

We do have the backstop there. We have Ofcom at the front end with the code of practice and we have Ofcom at the back end should that be necessary. We hope it will not be, but we have provided for that safeguard in the event. As the Minister said, these provisions are intended to support companies such as STV, given some of the challenges to which you allude.
Thank you for that clarification.
Q399 Thank you, Mr Specterman-Green .

Minister , w elcome. I asked you some questions last week when guesting in the Welsh Affairs Committee about radio. To take Mr Nicolson’s “Rocky Horror Picture Show” analogy, let’s do the time warp again. I will approach it a bit differently this time. You published a lengthy impact assessment about the Bill last week but you did not publish anything about radio in that impact assessment. Why?

We were still talking to the Regulatory Policy Committee about the radio provisions and we published an overarching assessment. The detailed impact assessment will be published when the Bill is published on introduction .

Q400 The Government asked us to perform scrutiny on this draft Bill. Can we effectively do that without sight of that? We have to produce our report before you publish that impact assessment. The idea is to publish it alongside not the final version but the version that you will introduce to the House. Does that hamper our ability to properly—

I am sorry in a way that we were not able to supply the Committee with the full impact assessment until quite late on in the process. There is quite a lengthy procedure within the Government to obtain agreement on the impact assessment, which we have now done. We have not yet finalised the radio provisions, which were a later part. I am keen that we should provide that as soon as we can.

Q401 You know the reason I ask. This part of the Bill has actually been the part that has produced a little bit of a spat in the evidence given to this Committee. We heard from representatives of the radio industry, who broadly welcome what the Government propose in the Bill. Then we heard from big tech in front of the Committee. It has not had regulation in any way of any kind ever, but it is not keen on what you propose as a Government.

Then we had a letter back as a Committee. I know you have not seen it, Minister, but it quite helpfully rebuts what big tech was saying to the Committee and lays out the five complaints that big tech was giving to this Committee. The easiest thing is if I put them to you and see what you think of the claims. The first is that there has been no consultation and insufficient research on the radio clauses — part 6 of the Bill. What is your response to that?

The provisions governing radio did not appear out of thin air. They came as a result of a lengthy digital radio and audio review, which we conducted. I was the Minister in my second incarnation when that review was conducted. Not only was that a lengthy discussion with representatives of the radio sector, but I know techUK was involved as well. The outcome of the review, which was recommendations that there should be protection for radio broadcasters on whatever devices are used, voice-activated devices, was agreed by all the participants in that, including techUK.
Q402 Charge 2: part 6, the radio clauses, is being rushed and should be dropped from the Media Bill.

Again, it has not been rushed. The radio review was published two or three years ago and there has been a lot of discussion since then. We have continued to consult. I had a roundtable with the tech platforms you are talking about yesterday and will continue to talk to them.
Q403 Charge 3: the regulation is unworkable in practice.

I do not see why it is unworkable. It is specifically targeted. Essentially—one of the points that we discussed yesterday—these are not regulations to require the sector to do something that it is not doing now. If it continues what it is doing now, it is fine. It is a preventive measure to stop it, for instance, suddenly imposing its own advertising instead of that which the broadcaster has agreed to broadcast , or to make it impossible to find. These are protective measures to ensure that radio is protected and accessible going forward. If it continues doing what it is doing now, there is not a problem.
Q404 Charge 4: it is unclear what is in scope of the regulation. We are getting a news bulletin as we speak.

The question as to which services and which devices are covered is one that we will develop, as in other parts of the Bill, in due course. Regulations are set down laying that out, which will be done by Ofcom subject to further consultation. When you said there has not been enough consultation, this is the beginning of the exercise and there will clearly be further consultation when they work out the details.
Q405 The final charge is that it will create a disincentive for innovation. That is always the charge laid with any regulation.

I do not see why it should. This does not impose any new requirement on them. As long as they do not want to do things that previously everybody had agreed would be undesirable, it should not have any impact on further research. It is true that innovation means that, as we were talking about earlier on TV content, the way in which people access radio content may well evolve in time. Therefore, you need the flexibility for the legislation to take account of that and that is there, but it is certainly not intended to prevent innovation.

Q406 I have a couple of technical questions to finish. We need the answers from you, too, as the Minister. I am loth, after what you said earlier on about significance, to use that word again , but this is in a different context. The Secretary of State can only designate radio selection services that are used by a significant number of people. What do you have in mind? What does “a significant number of people” mean?
I hesitate to say that 10,000 people is not significant whereas 100,000 is—
Sorry, Chair, could someone turn off that notification that keeps going off? I beg your pardon, Minister. It is irritating.

Clearly something dramatic is happening in the world outside. As I said, you cannot put a number on significance. To some extent, that will be a matter for the Secretary of State to determine on advice that will be received from Ofcom and Ofcom will provide advice or recommendations to the Secretary of State. To some extent, you will know significant when you see it.

Q407 Finally from me, why have the Government chosen not to further protect UK radio’s availability on connected audio devices to stations’ on-demand and online-only content as well? We heard some evidence about that earlier.

The provisions of the Bill are designed to cover the main stations and the way in which most people choose to access them. Most people still listen to live radio. There are other means, but at the moment we have not felt it necessary to extend these protections to those other means. We will see how the market develops. If it becomes clear that people access radio content on demand, which does not take place at the moment, we will need to revisit that.
Q408 Would it be sensible to put in the Bill a provision that would give the Secretary of State potentially the power to do that should that occur?
Robert, would the Secretary of State’s ability to designate new services cover that?

The powers in the Bill allow the Secretary of State to designate over a period of time. Should new information become available, and should Ofcom provide updated assessments of the market such that other selection services are advised to fall within the scope of the Bill, the Secretary of State can still make further designations. The focus of the Bill is device - neutral . We are looking more at the software, which is the voice - activation element of things.
Q409 Would that power include being able to revise the definition of an internet radio service?

Ofcom advises on the specific interpretation of that requirement in the Bill. If it changed, I imagine Ofcom could advise that this now was a method that was widely used and might merit inclusion in the Secretary of State’s powers.
Robert will run to the rescue.

I refer you to section 362BA, “Meaning of radio selection services”, which provides that the Secretary of State may do many things, including amend this section so as to alter the definition of a radio selection service. That answers your question [1] .

Q410 Can I push you back, Robert, on that comment about how it is focused on voice-activated systems? That does not scoop up others that are not voice-activated , such as those in cars. What is the plan for that?
Where car systems include voice - activation software, they will be in scope.
Q411 What about when they do not?
Then they will not be.
Q412 Does that concern you?
We try to target what we think to be the driver of future risk to radio. We need to target this gateway lever around voice - activation.

If they are not voice-activated , they are manually activated by the person who is listening. To that extent, they can choose. This is designed for where the software decides what you will listen to rather than you, almost. If you say, “I want to listen to this”, the software chooses how to deliver that.

Q413 I see. Briefly, I want to take you back to the video-on-demand issue. Why do only some video-on-demand providers have to abide by the code rather than all of them, as would be the case in the Broadcasting Code?

Mainly because there is a large number of video-on-demand services, some of which are small and watched by few people. It was felt important that where you had big services with a large number of subscribers, they should be subject not to the same requirements as laid down in the Broadcasting Code , but similar. Ofcom will in due course set out what those are and also the services that are covered. It will be the tier 1 services.

I was concerned when we originally looked at this that it should not restrict freedom of speech. There are some niche services on which it would be disproportionate to impose the full requirements of the code, which was designed to apply to services with substantial audiences.

Q414 Thank you. That has pretty much brought us to the end. Is there anything else that you think our Committee should take into consideration about the draft Bill that we have not had a chance to cover?

People have criticised us for the delay in drawing this up, but producing it as a draft Bill has advantages. It gives us the opportunity to get it right. One important contributor to that process will be your report. Thank you for undertaking the scrutiny you are doing. I can assure you that we will be keen to hear whatever recommendations the Committee comes back with.
Thank you both for being in front of us today and for your time. If there is anything else that you feel that we need to take into consideration before we wrap all this up, drop us a note.
We will let you know.

[1] Correction by witness: While it is correct that section 362 BA( 2) provides a power for the Secretary of State to revise the definition of a radio selection service, DCMS would like to clarify that this power does not extend to the definition of an internet radio service, and therefore the reference made to this section of the Bill does not answer the specific question asked by the Committee. In answer to the question on internet radio services, there is currently no power in the Bill to revise the definition of an internet radio service. The current definition of an internet radio service is tied to the existing licensing framework, reflecting that the core public value of radio is secured by that framework, and the Government does not consider that it is necessary at this stage to extend the scope of the measures in this Part of the Bill further than this.

sessions.w: Rethinking Assessment; The International Baccalaureate; Rethinking Assessment

segs.tx: Education for 11-16 Year Olds Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Education for 11-16 year olds
Thursday 29 June 2023
11 am
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Johnson of Marylebone (The Chair); Lord Aberdare; Lord Baker of Dorking; Baroness Evans of Bowes Park; Baroness Garden of Frognal; Lord Knight of Weymouth; Lord Lexden; Lord Mair; Lord Storey; Lord Watson of Invergowrie.
Evidence Session No. 12 Heard in Public Questions 119 - 12 7
Witnesses

I : Sarah Fletcher, High Mistress, St Paul’s Girls’ School, and Advisory Group Member, Rethinking Assessment; Matthew Glanville, Director of Assessment, The International Baccalaureate; Alistair McConville, Deputy Head, King Alfred School, and Co-Founder, Rethinking Assessment.
Examination of Witnesses
Sarah Fletcher, Matthew Glanville and Alistair McConville.

Q119 Good morning and welcome to this session of the Education for 11-16 Year Olds Committee. Welcome back, in the case of Sarah Fletcher. It is great to have you again with us. Thank you very much. As before, a transcript of the meeting will be taken and will be available for correction, should that be necessary. I would like to ask you each to quickly introduce yourselves, with just a line or so to say who you are and what your organisation is.

I am the high mistress, the head, at St Paul’s Girls’ School. I have taught and led numbers of schools abroad and at home, in the state sector as well as in the independent sector. I have always had a huge interest in educational reform and was particularly involved in the creation of the extended project qualification.

I am deputy head at King Alfred School, but also the co-founder of Rethinking Assessment, which is an organisation that is campaigning for assessment reform. It is not only campaigning but trying to show practical solutions to those problems. I have been a teacher of philosophy and religious studies in various independent schools—Cheltenham Ladies’ College, Latymer Upper School, Bedales and now King Alfred School.
I am the director for assessment at the IB , an international education organisation dealing with ages three to 18 . Our middle years programme is the one that is particularly pertinent today.

I apologise to the committee, but I need to put something on the record. At the Ofsted meeting, I blamed Ofsted for the fact that, at my daughter’s school, Ofsted arrived, the teachers were all geared up and Ofsted never talked to them at all. Amanda Spielman has now told me that that particular Ofsted inspection was concerned only with the procedures and paperwork of the senior staff, and she had told the senior staff that, but it was the senior staff who said to the teachers, “Come on . Ofsted’s coming. You’ve got to gear up”. So can I now apologise to Ofsted? On this occasion, it was not its fault, but the fault of the senior staff of the school.

Q120 Thank you. That is noted. I would like to kick off, please, with a question about GCSEs. In your view, are they fit for purpose , and h ow do the alternative key stage 4 qualifications that you offer differ from and/or complement them?

That is quite a big question. I do not think they are fit for purpose. It is interesting that they were introduced before the world wide web and before any school had computers. They were, therefore, looking at a different environment. We are working in a very different world now, and it is important that our qualifications be forward looking and give young people the skills they need for the modern world.

To me, GCSEs are what I call closed-box assessments. The information is given, and pretty much the answers that you are expected to give are given, because we need to be sure that answers are fair and easily moderated. Therefore, mark schemes, certainly latterly, have become a lot narrower ; students who display creativity and independence tend to find that those efforts are not rewarded, and they are possibly even penalised for that.

In a nutshell, the skills that we need young people to have for the modern world are not being developed in this type of examination. Typically, these exams are a terminal assessment at the end of the two-year course . They are in an exam room , solitary , and about memorisation. Although other skills are developed along the route, such as critical thinking, source analysis and understanding of quite difficult concepts, I would argue that the rigour of that kind of mental application is a lot less, because it is overweighted by the quantity of information you have to learn and the mode in which you have to recall and show your understanding, as in the terminal examination.

This is, ultimately, inequitable. Certainly post Covid, we have seen an increase in the number of students presenting as neurodiverse and asking for additional time and extra consideration in the exam room. As soon as you start seeing that grow to the extent that we have, you begin to understand that that terminal assessment is really not playing to the strengths of a significant number of our students.

Also, we are not preparing them for the world in which they will work. It is not just the world of work, but universities, which are increasingly asking students to do presentations, teamwork, collaborative open book assessments, computerised assessments and authentic assessments, which grappl e with complex problems. That is not what the GCSEs are training our young people to do, and so, going to university or into the workplace, they are not well equipped.

It is also a bigger issue than that. For me, it is about mental well-being and empowerment. The world is complicated and complex, and increasingly so, and young people need to have the critical faculties to understand that they too can change their environment, whether it is their own personal environment or engaging on a larger scale with the issues that are facing us. Therefore, it is incumbent on us to give them an education that enables them to do that. That does not mean an education that basically results in memorisation of a lot of information.

Our GCSEs and our discourse around education have promoted a very academic route between 14 and 16, and this has narrowed options for numbers of students for whom that is not their preferred way of working, and they do not see their ambitions lying in that direction. The creative and performing arts and technology have suffered significantly as a result, and it is time that we understood that all those things bring skills aplenty, and really important life skills at that, to young people, and that we rebalance the way we look at 14-16 education.

GCSEs impose stress. We know that the marking at the end of the period, with all the best intentions of every exam board, with strong moderation, can be variable. As Ofqual has said, a mark can be reliable to one grade either way, particularly in the more subjective subjects, the humanities, and yet we are using those marks as precise indicators of a student’s abilities. I would argue that that is unfair on two grounds. First, we know that they are not precise and, secondly, they are assessing only a very narrow range of those skills. We need to give young people the opportunity to show what they can do and how those skills will map on a much more successful future.

Finally, we also know that a third of all young people fail to get level 4 in English and maths, which really limits their life chances. I have to question not the young people but the system that enables that to happen.
We will come back to some of the alternatives a bit later on in the session, so I will press on and ask our other two panellists to comment on whether GCSEs are fit for purpose.

I would agree with everything that Sarah said about purpose and just pick up on that last point about a third failing. It was rather extraordinary to see Rishi Sunak bemoaning that fact recently without an apparent awareness that the system requires a third of people to fail every time. It is not possible for every child to pass their maths and English GCSE at age 16 because of the bell curve and the norm referencing that happens, so that was a bit alarming. If the purpose is to have everyone leave with a credible qualification about literacy and numeracy, they are certainly not.
Can I ask you to clarify your point about norm referencing and why a third have to fail , or have to get a 4 or below , in the system?

I am not a statistician, but there is a bell curve on to which a distribution of grades has to be fitted every year. Essentially, there is an allowance of grade 9s and grade 6s, and that bell curve is required to look roughly the same every year. A third of people necessarily fall into th e bottom third that are designated as failures. Officially, the exam boards would say, “That’s a pass . A 1, 2 or 3 is a pass”, but the Government define anything below a 4 as not a pass. A good pass is a 5, but the system requires a third of people to fail. Rather than using criterion referencing, which is more like a driving test where as many people as can demonstrate adequate competence will pass, there is an allowance of people who are allowed to pass.

I would invite the committee to ask exactly that question of Ofqual, because my understanding is that the GCSEs are based on a weak criterion referencing approach. I recognise some of the outcomes of what you are saying, but it perhaps is not quite as stark as that in the approach used. Again, I am a representative of the IB, so it is more appropriate that the regulator explains exactly how that system works.

You are right that there is a criterion referencing mini-moment where samples are compared to ensure that the bell curve roughly maps on to the standards of last year’s bell curve, but by far the overriding factor is getting this standard distribution of X numbers of grades. You could not suddenly have a great year when only 10% of people failed their English and maths. That is not possible because of the requirement to have the bell curve year on year.
Can I ask why the bell curve is even necessary? What is the purpose of it?
I am sure the answer would be that it is to ensure comparability year on year and to ensure that there is not grade inflation, essentially.
Ofqual receives a remit from the Secretary of State, and my understanding is that grade inflation is a substantial part of that remit, but we can ask Ofqual about that.
Aside from th e problem of sorting too many people into that category of failing because of the bell curve, did you have any general reflections about whether GCSEs are fit for purpose?

If you take a more positive definition of the purpose of education and try to be more holistic in what you say education is for—at my last school, for example, we talked about head, hand and heart to try to demonstrate the roundedness of development that we wanted education to deliver—then, no, it fails. It offers only one small part of a rounded education.

The GCSE experience is very head-focused in those terms. Particularly if you have a standard nine or 10-GCSE experience it is all about head knowledge and leaves very little time for the development of other important elements of an education, such as crucial skills that will help people succeed at the next level , which Sarah has alluded to . At my current school, King Alfred, we talk about the need to develop communication, collaboration and creative thinking skills. There is an opportunity cost to spending all your time on knowledge and understanding, leaving very little time to develop the broad character measures that we know matter so much.

In a balanced wheel of education, you might have the knowledge and understanding bit, the character bit and the skills bit, but the number of GCSEs that are required in an ordinary school is so large that there is simply not the space to do all the things that we would like our children to be doing and to be recognised and have validation for. It is one very narrow bit of what an education should be , and it is assessed in a way that is not really fair, because some people are good at those sorts of demonstrations of knowledge and understanding , and others would do far better if they were able to explain orally, for example, that they have understood something about a great work of literature. How exam-focused it is, particularly since the 2015 reforms, has made it a very narrow opportunity to demonstrate even the thing that it is all about, which is knowledge and understanding.

What the IB attempts to do is very similar to what we have heard described. MYP is one of the alternatives to GCSEs that you have spoken about. It is that effort to focus on the conceptual understanding, giving those students the chance to show their thinking skills in unfamiliar situations, the interdisciplinary element and the creative problem-solving element.

We have an assessment moment for each student at the end of the MYP. For several of those subjects, that is through a digital assessment. For others, it is through an e-portfolio approach, depending on whether the approach is right. A key part of the middle years programme is a personal project, where the student has a chance to develop something that is personal to them, and the IB reviews that. That gives you an idea of some of the other options that are possible.

To your specific question, the GCSE assessments are broadly delivering on what they are being asked to deliver on. It is important to look at the whole-system educational context to understand why GCSEs are behaving in the way they do.

Q121 It is credible to argue that GCSEs examine the national curriculum, which runs to 16. Therefore, you can have an argument with the curriculum rather than with the GCSEs, which are doing the job they have been asked to do. Should we have exams at 16? At St Paul’s, you have GCSEs and IGCSEs, which you choose to do. At King Alfred’s you do the same, as you did at Bedales. You have the MYP, which gives way to the diploma programme at 16. You all choose to have exams at 16, yet many jurisdictions do not, so why should we, when we no longer allow people to leave school altogether at 16, examine at 16?

You raise a really good point. The MYP exams are optional, for exactly that reason : t hey are there for the schools that wish to have them, but it is quite possible to finish the curriculum without doing anything other than the personal project exercise, which is a requirement, because we think the process of doing that really helps a student to understand and develop. It is also a bit of a celebration when they reach 16.

It is a really good question. In the UK system, those grades are deeply embedded at the moment, which is why the MYP serve s that need. If that information is not required, or if this could be done better by informing the student rather than the system about that student’s strengths and weaknesses, which would then go to alternative ways of measuring it, that could be a really interesting approach to look at.

I do not think that exams have any kind of intrinsic evil in them at that point. There needs to be assessment all the way through a student’s career to tell them how they are doing and what they need to do better. The real problem is the number of exams all happening with in a tiny window, the stakes that are attached to that very large number of exams, and the fact that it is only exams that tell us how a student is supposedly doing.

It is entirely reasonable to have some examination if the stakes are proportionate and if there are other balancing sources of information to tell people how students are doing. Students tell us that sitting 30 or so exams in June is an incredibly stressful experience at a time of their maximally sensitive development as adolescents. Their brains are all over the place. Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, professor of psychology at Cambridge, is really clear that we are doing something to young people that is time and development-inappropriate. They are saying, “This is harming us. This is why we are among the unhappiest adolescents in the developed world and why there is this epidemic of teenage anxiety”. At a self-reported level, this is the thing we are doing to them that is really problematic.

I agree a lot with what Al has said. We need to be careful about what the word “exam” means. If we define it simply as sitting solo at a desk and writing, as it currently stands, we need to rethink it. However, if we are looking at assessment as a broader piece, a lighter-touch assessment at 16-plus is perfectly reasonable.

We also need to have a look at the purpose of assessment. Most assessment should be for the student and should be around touchpoints as to how well they are doing, encouragement to do things differently and better, and rewarding what they have done really well.

I also understand that there needs to be accountability. We need to be careful that we define assessment in different ways and do not necessarily make all the assessment the same. Currently, for example, all assessment is used as an accountability measure for schools, Progress 8. That means to say that every bit is what I might call high-stakes assessment. There is every merit in looking at how we can assess differently so that we are mixing the varieties and making it much more student focused .

Q122 I agree with everything that you have said. The case against GCSEs is formidable, but we must have an effective alternative. You talk of assessment. Presumably that would start in the primary school and a record would be built up over the years as they go from primary into secondary up to 16. Would it be necessary for that assessment to have maybe written tests at a school level in English and maths? The two basic skills of writing and reading have to be tested effectively at some stage . How would you achieve that? Would you go along with that sort of idea?

All the things you have said about recording a child’s record are absolutely right. We have used AI already in the assessment of children taking technical work in our colleges, and we find it as accurate as the teachers, if I may say, and better because it also provides student prompts. I would like your idea as to where there should be some sort of written test, not at a national level but at the school, in basic literacy and numeracy.
I would probably add digital literacy to that, but I agree entirely.

I agree that there needs to be evidence of achievement, which may or may not be achieved by a silent test, or it could just be accumulated classwork or a portfolio. There certainly needs to be evidence of the development of literacy and numeracy.
The skills that you described are well assessed in an exam context, but there is also verbal communication , which would need to be assessed in a different way.

Q123 Like Lord Baker, I agree with what you have been saying, but I have a challenge. During the pandemic, we saw teacher assessment that led to inflation of grades. On non-exam assessments, how do we ensure reliability and that it is the pupil’s own work? My wife was a secondary teacher and, at the time, it was sometimes just a tick-box exercise to make sure that that pupil got the grade the school wanted them to get, so that they got a good result at the end, which could go in to their prospectus, et cetera. How do we ensure that parents and employers have confidence in a continual assessment approach as opposed to formal written exams?

We can ensure that teacher marks are consistent across schools through the moderation process. That is the way the IB currently deals with the coursework elements we have. It is about selecting a random element from the teacher’s marking and making sure that our examiners agree with the marks that the teacher has given and the reasons why. That can be done.

The academic integrity issue is a very interesting one. The people who are best placed to understand whether it is the student’s own work are, of course, the teachers. If we have a system whereby the pressure on the teacher is not to maximise the student’s grade but to represent the result accurately, that can work. We can also do it with the way in which we select the questions. The “why” questions in an assessment are much harder for a student to get somebody or something else to do, rather than just doing it themselves.
Would that mean we would have to remove some of the other pressures that schools and teachers face to ensure that we get a reliable assessment?

There is certainly a real tension at the moment in the role of teachers. Is it to maximise the student’s performance, to maximise the school’s performance, or to be the guardian of a high-quality education?

On the teacher assessment experience, it is important to be clear that that was not comparing apples with apples, because the requirement for that standardisation process, whereby everything is fitted on to a bell curve, was removed during that period. So w hat you had was teachers’ best judgments about a child’s best performance, not on a given day. In a way, there was an inbuilt optimism to it that removed the possibility of kids having a shocking day on an exam.

It is not that teachers inflated grades ; i t was a different system. When Ofqual went to do its own moderation of schools to see whether these things had been reasonably applied, it made very few changes indeed. Its scrutiny of the teacher assessments, given the slightly different system under which teachers were operating, essentially said, “You’ve got this right”. It was as though we had moved to a criteri on -based system from a norm-based system, and that enabled many students to do better, which is a good thing.

Teachers were not prepared for that experience. Training was not given for that assessment. Those of us who see a lot of merit in training teachers up to do good and reliable teacher assessment would say that that was not a totally fair set of evidence to use to compare. Therefore, “grade inflation” is not the right term for that. It was a different system.

To go back to how you ensure reliability in a teacher assessment world, there are good systems where you would have school-to-school moderation processes to support one another in arriving at the right sorts of judgments. I agree that teachers deserve to be trusted. They are professionals. If the stakes are not unreasonable around this stuff, you do not create the scenario in which people are much more likely psychologically to game the system. There is an interplay between the stakes around this stuff for individual teachers and for schools, which relates to accountability measures, and their ability to do their job professionally without undue pressures on them.

It depends on the task that you are setting the student and how you phrase your questions. The extended project qualification, for example, rewards the process more than the outcome. This is important for reliability and for deep - thinking skills. The EPQ insists that the student has a literature log. They have to log their thought processes. They have to comment on how a particular piece of evidence has altered their way of thinking and how it has potentially impacted the way they framed their own question. Therefore, when they produce the final piece, there is a huge amount of evidence that shows that they have put the work into it and not somebody else. The extended project qualification also comes hand in hand with a presentation, and I would find it very difficult for a student to plagiarise and then stand up and present convincingly in front of quite a critical crew of their own peers and other members of staff.

O ur school-directed art course is another example . W e teach a module on history of art. The students then have to write a piece of coursework that is to do with a chosen element . The framing of the question is the important point here. Earlier in the course, they will have done various assessed pieces of practical work that are personal, so when they come to write their essay about history of art it is about how their personal projects fit in to the context and the analysis of art history. I would defy any ChatGPT to be able to replicate something that is quite so personal.
If you are a student whose first language is not English, you are immediately at a disadvantage, particularly if you live in a deprived community and are struggling to make ends meet.

No, not necessarily, because the extended project approach does not necessarily rely upon a written answer. You can produce all sorts of things. You can produce an object. You can create something. You can put on a play.

To continue on how you ensure reliability, as a teacher you will have given the students time in class to complete their assignment . You have not said, “Go away and do it”. In class, you are acting as a mentor and a guide. You are scaffolding the pupil and helping them, but you are also seeing their thought processes and marking that. Most of the mark s are not for the end product but the process, and that is really important.

Q124 I should have declared an interest. I am also a member of Rethinking Assessment. Alistair, I am very impressed with the group that is working on research. They now have lots of experiments going on in all sorts of different schools across the country. What is emerging from those? Will you be able to develop an emerging example that deals with the questions that concern other people, the overoptimism of teachers and things of this sort? How can it be standardised reasonably over the country?

Rethinking Assessment is working on a number of things. I will mention one or two of them. Our overarching solution to the problem is a digital learner portfolio, which is a way of capturing a broad range of evidence of achievements, some of which might be standardised achievements similar to current GCSEs. This is also a way of capturing other kinds of achievements that are assessed in different ways. School-directed courses, for example, could sit with in a digital learner portfolio. They will inevitably vary from one another in the way they are assessed and are standardised, but you can provide information about the way that process happens for that channel of learning.

For us, the solution is to have a mixture of different types of evidence, some of which might be highly standardised and of interest to certain audiences, which want to know that it is utterly reliable and comparable to every other school in the country, as with English and maths GCSE perhaps. I recognise that this other sphere of learning, which enables them to develop broader skills that are difficult to standardise but are really important for them to be engaging in, has a different level of comparability. Some of the workstreams in Rethinking Assessment are about developing reliable criteria for demonstrations of creativity or communication. There are well-researched models for what good oral communication looks like, which Voice 21 has done a lot on. Withi n this broad capture of a student’s overall experience and achievements, you would have written exam results, for those for whom that was interesting, as well as evidence of good speaking, which you can scale.
Yes, communication.
Absolutely .
Would the student be able to access that and add to it if they wanted to?

Yes. In our vision, this is a cumulative thing. It does not simply have to be handed in when you are 16. You build it up and curate it over time. It is validated externally as you go along and can be taken beyond school. Essentially, it is akin to but not the same as the very good notion of the record of achievement from all those years ago, but with all the advantages that technology now confers on us to make that adaptable, reliable and filterable for different audiences.

Q125 I have been interested for some time in the Bedales assessed qualifications, but you are all innovators in this area. What are the barriers to alternative assessments being adopted by a large number of state - maintained, state-funded schools in particular at key stage 4, and how could we overcome them?

Progress 8 is a huge barrier to schools being able to do courses on their own. The other thing relates to university protocols and the feeling that you have to serve up a certain number of GCSEs and A-levels in order to fulfil that process. There are also issues to do with teacher workload, teacher training, and time and resources, and we have already had allusion to that. There are ways of overcoming all those things, but they are significant barriers that we need to think about.

I also come back to the issue of confidence in grading , which we have talked about . It is important that when we are looking at how to reform this system , we keep that really clear in our minds. Whatever we do has to have the confidence of parents, students, universities and employers. There are a whole number of constituent groups that this has to resonate with if we are to succeed.

I recommend that we create a system where we have assessment in different forms and that we accept that there are different levels of reliability . W here we have school-directed courses they must b e externally moderated, as all of ours are. There are ways of doing that better. There are ways of engaging with universities and with employers on how we do this. There is also an enormous opportunity to get schools to work together in consortia, which would be hugely beneficial in sharing good practice, ideas and resources, a s well as in moderating each other’s work.

The exam boards should play a role in this as well. Whatever courses we adopt, I would like to see a baccalaureate, rather like the IB middle years programme, where you have your national curriculum on the one hand , and on the other you have your modes of assessment and the skills associated with them. As Al point s out, there are ways you can assess communication and critical thinking in the logs and the other bits of evidence that you are asking students to produce.

The exam boards are then part of a process , picking out bits of work to moderate in order to make sure that the consortia and the individual schools are sticking to the overarching rubric. Schools then have the opportunity to put together the national curriculum, potentially in a cross-curricular , interdisciplinary way , or in a much more subject-specific way, depending on their own students and their own approaches. This would free up the system, provided you also have a core of standard assessment , which all schools do, which plays to the point about English, maths and potentially digital skills. It is crucial that thes e assessments should be delivered, examined and assessed in a way that, again, holds the utmost public confidence.

You mentioned the university protocols. From the conversations you have had with the universities as you have developed your own qualifications and assessments, do you get the sense that they respect the content that is assessed in GCSEs and then in A-levels, or do they just really like fact that it does their admissions job for them in selecting people?

That will vary according to subject. Your sciences and maths may well have a different answer to your humanities subjects. At GCSE, that is more of a moot point. At A-level, perhaps that matters rather more. P articularly if you are looking at geography, history or all of the humanities, I do not think that it really matters what content you study. It is your mindset ; the way you analyse material and the way you think matter far more than a particular canon.

Perhaps I should start by saying what the School Directed Courses Consortium is and then a tiny bit about why it might be difficult for some schools to do it. This is a consortium of schools that are either already running their own GCSE alternatives—St Paul’s Girl’s, Bedales, King Alfred School and others—and schools that would really like to get into that world. Some have already committed to doing it and others have not yet committed because of the barriers. The group exists for us to support one another, and , for those of us who are more experienced , to help those who want to do it in taking that first step towards the development of their own courses.

The barriers for schools that would desperately love to do this are, as Sarah says, primarily Progress 8 and EBacc measures. They have concerns about being judged negatively by Ofsted for doing something a little offbeat, as well as concerns about teacher expertise, because teachers are now very good at delivering their GCSEs, but that is not the same as developing their own curriculum and applying new assessment methodologies.

Very frequently, you will have highly enthusiastic senior management teams and highly wary heads of department who are saying, “Hang on a minute . T hat sounds like a heck of a lot of work”—not that they are afraid of lots of work, but they already have lots of work—“so how are you going to help us get there?” The consortium exists to smooth the way for them to do that, so there is a possibility that we could do joint course design. We are already freely sharing the materials that we have for our courses with anyone who wants to look at that stuff, so that they could pick it up and do it.

Then there are the barriers of external audiences such as parents, who are often the most conservative, as are the students themselves sometimes, about doing something new-fangled ; t hey do not always want to be the guinea pigs.
I am glad you have raised that question about parents and an interesting quote that they are “often the most conservative” — with a small C, I assume. What are the arguments that shift them?

They are very shiftable. When I speak to parents, they understand that students need certain tokens of exchange, which is what I call the GCSEs and the A-levels, to do their course at university and are very anxious that t hese should be in place. They are also very aware that the world has changed, and that GCSEs are inappropriate. There are no two ways about that. When I talk to them about what I am saying here and generally about my attitude towards these things, there is almost universal support.
So they would have an appetite for a different token of exchange.

Yes, very much so, but that is not simple. I have spoken in many other environments, including when I was head at City boys’, to lots of academy heads. They had exactly the same response: the parents know that the world has changed, but also that they have to have these exams because they have to.

That is very helpful. Matthew , I am interested in your answer to the substantive question, but, in particular, a long time ago Andrew Adonis and I, as Schools Ministers, agreed to fund the IB diploma programme so that it was available in every local authority area. It has subsequently been defunded, and I am just interested in your relationship, as the International Baccalaureate organisation , with the Department for Education, and the appetite that state-funded schools might have to use your qualifications and get them funded.

As people have said, the barrier s are the funding, the EBacc and Progress 8. We speak regularly with the Department for Education and regularly try to explain to it why we believe that the IB education philosophy, whether it is the MYP level or the DP level, benefits schools, and to highlight situations where it has been very successful, not in the state school system, where it is not funded, but in the private school system in the UK. We are constantly trying to talk to the d epartment to see whether there is any opportunity to allow schools to have this alternative route and one that is well understood.

Do you think that its antipathy, assuming that that is what it is, is that it is just too awkward to work out how to make it fit in the accountability system, or is it something deeper than that that means they do not want to fund it? It might be the cost. You might be ridiculously expensive, for all I know.

I am not able to read the minds of the Ministers and officials who are currently preventing it. There is a certain desire at the moment for the flagship education process to be the English education system, rather than adapting something else. For everybody who wants to offer something different, there is a challenge. A lot of what we are also trying to do is to flag why what we are doing is very good and to help to explain why IB elements can be adopted.

Post 16, as well as the diploma programme, the IB offers a more vocational programme. Do you ever consider a more vocational track to the MYP or do you think that it covers off vocational, technical and academic—or head, heart, hand, however you choose to describe it ?

What we really want our 11 to 16-year-olds to be learning can be done with in the framework of the MYP at the moment. It is a framework rather than a curriculum in some sense, which means that our schools have more opportunities, as long as they are delivering on the thinking skills and the examples of how it is all interlinked. That is the opportunity there. For schools that need the academic element, we offer the MYP assessment at the end. I do not think we would go down the route of a vocational MYP e-assessment at the moment, because that is not a skillset that we have.

T here are rigorous and academically meaningful ways of testing some of the broader range of skills that we have talked about. I do not want us to relegate those agile problem-solving skills to the “un ‑ assessable” space. We can; it is more challenging . B ut you should be holding us and Ofqual to account for being able to do that.

Q126 We have already touched on AI a few times. I want to ask you more about the opportunities for greater use of technology, both for education and for assessment —they obviously go together. What are the opportunities? Will the assessment methods need to adapt to evolving technologies? What are the challenges and risks?

Can I start with an opportunity? I am working with a wonderful organisation that is seeking to make its publications available, and it has already signed with Penguin Random House. This is not open AI; it is closed. It is intended to produce a programme that will help to close the literacy gap, and it is superb. It enables children in primary school s and right the way through to state their preferences in terms of topics and reading materials , and the AI will produce for them accessible, relevant examples of reading that will appeal to them and help to improve their literacy. Their teachers can play a part in how this develops too.

It includes grammatical constructs and vocabulary—all the sorts of things that teachers are wanting to develop. It could provide every family that this will be available to, once it is up and running, with open access to all the publications of Penguin Random House, which is phenomenal. AI can do that in reading and mathematics. We have an enormous possibility here to close learning gap s and to make a huge difference to the education of our young people through the use of AI, and we need to seize that.

On opportunities for assessment, there seems to be more scepticism about how well AI can mark complicated essays. Perhaps we are not there yet. It is very good at marking shorter answers; it is less good at creativity. I do not necessarily think that we should put a cap on it, but we should be careful not to run before we can walk. We also need to be very careful that there is proper regulation around it, because if we are going to assess young people using AI, we have to be very sure that the algorithms at its root and the way it is developed are genuinely equitable and assessing the skills that we want them to assess. There must be caution, but the opportunities are immense.
So what you have just said are the challenges and risks.

The other challenge and risk is what everyone is talking about with ChatGPT, which is the opportunity for plagiarism and cheating. A much bigger risk to education and, in fact, to everything is the whole issue of truth and what can feed into it , which can create conspiracy theories and all sorts of falsehoods, which will create a massive problem beyond schools. There are real challenges with the way AI is developing.

There are solutions to th e issue of plagiarism . I have already given you one example of how we are framing questions in our school-directed courses so that AI cannot do them. I n our creative technologies course, which we have developed ourselves, the students produce coursework precisely on the ethical issues surrounding technology. They do it under controlled conditions. We run through ChatGPT how it would answer the question, and we give it to the students and say, “There you are. You can incorporate that in the way you think about and analyse the problems”. In other words, use it for what it is best used for. Rather than hide, bring it into the open. It is very clear then that they are using it positively rather than as a piece of plagiarism. We have to be clever about how we frame and ask questions. We should not deny generative AI . We should use it and embrace it, but be aware of the risks.

I will be brief on this, because it is not my area of expertise. One obvious benefit is the potential individualisation of each child’s experience. There are already really good AI-driven platforms to help to move students’ learning on. There is a programme called Century Tech that adapts to a child’s demonstration of their knowledge through a learning platform and takes them on to the most appropriate bit. The development of those sorts of learning tools is really exciting.

As far as assessment goes, the thing I am most interested in at the moment is comparative judgment and the use of technology to support it . It is very difficult to get two people to agree which out of two essays should be a 17 or an 18, but it is quite easy to get people to agree on which one is better, oddly, and therefore easy to rank things based on quite holistic judgments. Technology is enabling that to happen much more quickly now, even enabling the ranking of portfolios based on holistic judgments so that even where something is quite disparate in its component parts you can quite quickly get to judgments, when necessary, about which are in the top quartile or the second quartile. That is very interesting.

The most important point is that, since their inception, the MYP assessments have been digital. That allows us to start testing things that are really important to test and that you cannot do on a blank piece of paper. It allows you to have that interactive experience. In sciences, for example, it allows the student to control which variables vary, rather than almost giving them the answer and asking them to spot it. With video technology and 3D images, there is so much more that we can do using digital assessments to really focus on what is important on the assessment side. I am a huge advocate of that. It is also the way our students interact at the moment. The key thing there, though, is that we also need that to filter into how the students experience learning and education in the classroom, so there are huge possibilities there.

We have summed up very nicely that artificial intelligence will be a reality for many of our students in the future, so we need to teach them what ethical use looks like. That is why the IB has not banned its use but said, “Please use it but reference it properly”. There is great opportunity in the marking. I am still not confident enough that it will mark effectively, but once we get to that point, and I am sure we will, that opens up opportunities for things like adaptive testing.

What we must not do with digital is have a race to the bottom. We must not allow it to go to narrow multiple choice or drag and drop. At the moment, adaptive testing requires instant marking, which can be done only if it is a narrow right/wrong answer. In the future, if artificial intelligence can mark for us, maybe we can start to use it . The advantages of adaptive testing mean that you give the students the tests that show what they can do, rather than giving them opportunities to muck up what they do not need to do.

I am very glad that you mentioned comparative judgment. That is a really powerful, different way of assessing , which the IB has been exploring, particularly with our theory of knowledge, which is the classic one: “It’s very hard to agree on what the mark is, but very easy to agree on what’s a good or a bad answer”. It is really about how we reflect the way young people learn, engage and see things. A paper exam is just so foreign to them. Indeed, we have schools where the poor students have to learn how to write a three-hour essay by hand again, because they have got used to word processing and everything else.

On th at point, I agree entirely with you. I went into a class in one of my UTCs. They were doing GCSE exams and they were all doing it on their computers.
